extractionWhich of the town's two FY2023 statements of what the special revenue and enterprise funds held is right?The FY2023 combined balance sheet gives special revenue fund equity as 6,131,303.68 and enterprise fund equity as 3,812,502.24, together 9,943,805.92. The special revenue schedule in the SAME annual report prints a grand total carried forward of 10,031,099.78. They are 87,293.86 apart. The comparison ties to the cent in FY2011, FY2013, FY2019 and FY2022, and the balance sheet's own arithmetic is complete -- every column foots to its own printed totals and liabilities plus equity equals assets -- so this is two published tables disagreeing and not a reading error. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2023 trial balance, which would say which of the two the books support.
heldHow much of each grant and revolving fund the schools left unspent at the end of each yearThe school general fund's unspent money is its Left, and the circuit breaker's is what the budget book counted on less what was charged; both are drawn on /school-all-funds/fy-breakdown. No other school fund has an allocation for the year in the books we hold. The period-13 special funds report prints a revised budget for a handful of grants only (FY2026: a few hundred thousand dollars against millions spent from other funds), and money RECEIVED in a year is not an allocation either: IDEA is reimbursed after it is spent, so FY2026's IDEA receipts print as nothing. What a revolving fund or a grant had left at 30 June is a fund balance, and we hold special revenue balances only at period 9 of FY2026. — closes: the Town's special revenue fund balance report (or trial balance) at period 13 for each school fund, FY2023-FY2026, beside each grant's award letter for the award year.
heldHow much the Special Education Reserve Fund holds, and what the law lets it doSpecial Town Meeting on 18 November 2025 accepted Mass. General Laws chapter 40 section 13E and established a Special Education Reserve Fund for unanticipated or unbudgeted special education, out-of-district tuition and transportation costs (FY2025 annual town report). The Town Manager told the Select Board on 7 October 2025 that spending from it needs a majority of both the School Committee and the Select Board and that its balance may not exceed 2% of annual net school spending. The statute itself is not in this archive, so the cap and the vote are as described at a meeting; and no balance, deposit or withdrawal is in any ledger held here. The School Committee's agenda for 7 October 2026 carries an item to vote an amount to fund it. — closes: the text of chapter 40 section 13E (malegislature.gov, public); and the Treasurer's balance of the fund with every vote to fund or spend it, from the Town Accountant.
heldWhat spending the general Stabilization Fund would do to the town’s borrowingThe town’s reserves are one of the things a rating agency weighs, and this archive holds NO bond rating for Lunenburg, no rating report, and no official statement from any bond issue — so what the rating is, what any agency has said about the reserves, and what a downgrade would cost per million borrowed are all unknown here. The question is live and has been asked in public: at the Finance Committee on 13 March 2025 a resident asked whether not contributing to OPEB affects the town’s bond rating, and the minutes record the question and no reply. Until this closes, any sentence about "what the rating agencies would think" is a hypothesis, including on /analysis/stabilization-option, which says so. — closes: the official statement for the town’s most recent bond issue, and the rating agency report that accompanied it, both of which the Treasurer holds.
heldWhat the $102,000.00 is that the FY2024 enterprise balance sheet classifies two ways at onceThe Combining Balance Sheet - Enterprise Funds in the FY2024 annual town report — printed twice, on printed pages 21 and 28, identically — prints 'Reserved for expenditures' as 400,000.00 in the Sewer column and 502,000.00 in the Totals (Memorandum Only) column, and prints 'Unreserved retained earnings' as 2,973,842.15 in the memorandum column where the four fund columns (1,813,817.53 Sewer, 51,333.93 Water, 181,853.82 Solid Waste, 1,028,836.87 PEG Access) add to 3,075,842.15. The memorandum column is $102,000.00 high on the first line and $102,000.00 low on the second, so the two cancel and Total Fund Equity (3,483,633.65), Total Assets, the identity and the sheet's own printed PROOF row all still tie in every column — compensating errors, invisible to any check that reads only totals. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: which presentation is right, or what the $102,000.00 is. A reservation sitting in a fund column that prints blank, a memorandum column keyed to a different worksheet row, and a reclassification made only in the total column all fit the same signature, and nothing on the page distinguishes them. These are ratepayer funds; nothing here is general-fund money. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2024 trial balance for the enterprise funds, which would state the reserved and unreserved balance of each fund separately.
heldWhat the $87,293.86 is that the FY2023 annual report states twice and differentlyTwo tables printed in the same FY2023 annual town report state the money held in special revenue and enterprise funds, and they disagree. The combined balance sheet on printed page 24 gives TOTAL FUND EQUITY of $6,131,303.68 for SPECIAL REVENUE and $3,812,502.24 for ENTERPRISE, $9,943,805.92 together. The special revenue schedule in the same report prints a GRAND TOTAL carried forward of $10,031,099.78. The difference is $87,293.86, where FY2011, FY2013, FY2019 and FY2022 agree to the cent. It is not a misreading: the FY2023 page was transcribed and every column foots to its own printed TOTAL ASSETS, TOTAL LIABILITIES and TOTAL FUND EQUITY, the accounting identity holds in all six columns, and the long-term debt mirror agrees. So FY2023 is transcribed and deliberately NOT written into the dataset, which is why the combined balance sheet here stops at FY2022 while the special revenue schedule runs to FY2023. One explanation has been tested and RULED OUT: the fund 'Sale of Cemetery Lots' carried $87,308.09 in FY2023, within $14.23 of the gap, which suggested a fund counted in one statement and classified elsewhere in the other. It is not that — the same fund appears in the schedule in all thirteen years including the four where the two documents agree to the cent, so it is counted consistently and the near-match is a coincidence. What the difference IS remains unestablished; nothing here says which document is right, nor whether it is connected to the $17,861.24 of grant funds the town restated between the FY2022 and FY2023 reports. Those are two different amounts and nothing joins them. — closes: the Town's FY2023 trial balance or general ledger fund balances as of 30 June 2023, which would say which of its own two published tables the accounting system agrees with.
heldWhat the PEG Access enterprise fund actually held at 30 June 2025Three figures for the same fund on the same date appear in the same FY2025 annual town report and no document in this archive prints a line between any two of them. The PAC report's FY25 REVENUE vs EXPENSES table (printed page 60, pdf 64) gives an Ending Balance of $30,632, computed on its own face as Beginning Balance $208,772 less Expenses $178,140 -- and the prose beside it says the $208,772 was "the budget starting balance", so the ending balance is unspent spending authority rather than money. The Treasurer's Cash schedule in the same report prints Bartholomew- PEG Access Enterprise Fund 782,591.31$. The Combining Balance Sheet - Enterprise Funds (printed page 21, pdf 25) prints PEG Access Total Fund Equity of $1,072,661.74, against $1,028,836.87 the year before -- a rise of $43,824.87, where the statement's own revenue less expenses is $262,565 - $178,140 = $84,425. The two do not reconcile and nothing on either page relates them. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: which quantity any of the three is; a budget balance, a bank balance and a fund equity are three different things and the report labels none of them as such. -- closes: the Town Accountant's FY2025 year-end statement of revenues, expenditures and changes in fund balance for the PEG Access and Cable Related Enterprise Fund, which the annual report does not contain.
heldWhat the Sewer Reserve Capacity and Arts Lottery funds held at 30 June 2023The FY2023 annual town report prints each of these balances TWICE, in two different tables, and the two printings disagree. TRUST AND STABILIZATION FUNDS HELD BY OTHER BANKS (pdf page 49) gives SEWER RESERVE CAPACITY (UNIBANK) an ENDING CASH VALUE of $28,144.20 and ARTS LOTTERY (MMDT) $19,120.90. Treasurer's Cash as of 6/30/2023 (pdf page 48) gives Unibank Sewer Capacity Reserve Stabilization $28,144.50 and Mass Municipal Depository Trust (MMDT) Arts Lottery $19,121.07. NEITHER IS A MISREADING: each column foots to its own printed total to the cent -- page 49's eleven funds sum to the printed GRAND TOTALS of $2,363,536.23, and page 48's thirty-nine accounts sum to the printed Total Treasurer Cash of $27,244,162.79 -- so the report disagrees with itself by $0.30 and $0.17. Six other funds appear on both pages and match exactly, which is what makes the two the odd ones rather than the tables a different measure. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: which of the two each pair is. An ending cash value on a custodian's trust statement and a treasurer's cash balance are produced by different parties on different books and the report relates them nowhere, so the difference may be a posting date, an accrual, or a typing error in one of them, and nothing here can tell those apart. The amounts are small; the pattern is not, because these two tables are the only two statements of these balances the town publishes and they are printed in every annual report. -- closes: the Treasurer's year-end reconciliation of cash to the custodian's statements at 30 June 2023, which the annual report does not contain.
heldWhat the school grant funds held at 30 June 2024, 2025 and 2026Fourteen school funds -- circuit breaker, school choice, lunch, eight fee-funded revolving funds and three gift funds -- are carried from the annual report's 30 June 2023 balance through the MUNIS period-13 ledgers, and the result ties to the cent to the Town's March 2026 special revenue report for every one. The grant funds cannot be carried that way: the annual report names a grant by programme and year, MUNIS numbers it, and nothing published maps one to the other; and a reimbursement grant spends before it is paid, so one year's revenue less expense is not a change in what it holds. So the school total after 2023 covers the fourteen and not the grants. Measured in /analysis/sitting-on-money. — closes: a MUNIS fund balance report at period 13 for the school grant funds (26xx-29xx), FY2024 to FY2026, with each fund's opening and closing balance.
heldWhat the school revolving funds and the circuit breaker held at 30 June 2026The FY2023 annual town report prints each school special revenue fund's balance carried; the school journal gives every receipt and payment since. /school-all-funds/unspent-by-fund rolls the first forward with the second, and that is OUR arithmetic, not a balance anybody printed: it assumes the journal holds every receipt (one fund's interest is booked outside the school department) and it does not take off orders still open. The FY2024 and FY2025 annual reports' special revenue schedules are held and not yet read. — closes: the Town Accountant's special revenue fund balances at 30 June 2024, 2025 and 2026, school funds.
heldWhat the town held town-wide at 30 June 2024 and 30 June 2025The FY2024 and FY2025 annual town reports print NO combined balance sheet across all fund types and account groups — the schedule the reports carried every year from FY2011 to FY2023. In both editions the table of contents lists 'Balance Sheet for FY Ending June 30, 2024' at Page 21 and 'Balance Sheet for FY Ending June 30, 2025' at Page 21 respectively, and printed page 21 of each holds the Combining Balance Sheet - Enterprise Funds instead; FY2024 prints that enterprise sheet a second time on page 28, which is where its contents page says it should be. So for two consecutive years the only balance sheet the town published covers four ratepayer enterprise funds and says nothing about the general fund, special revenue, capital projects, trust and agency, or long-term debt. The consequence is that the general fund's cash, receivables, reserves and undesignated fund balance — the figures free cash is built out of — cannot be read for either year, and the balance_sheet dataset stops at FY2023 for that reason rather than by choice. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the town-wide sheet was produced and dropped in layout or never produced; nothing in either report says. — closes: the Town Accountant's year-end balance sheet submitted to the Division of Local Services for FY2024 and FY2025, or the town's audited financial statements for those years.
heldWhat the town’s own special revenue funds held at 30 June 2024, 2025 and 2026The annual town reports print every special revenue fund's balance at 30 June, and this project has read and proved FY2011 to FY2023 -- forward, receipts, disbursements and carried, every row and every printed GRAND TOTAL tying (special-revenue-read.csv). FY2024 and FY2025 print a DIFFERENT table, a balance detail with no receipts or disbursements, no row identity and no stable fund key: it is printed and has not yet been read into a dataset, which is our gap rather than the town's. FY2026's annual report is not yet published. The school side of 'is anyone sitting on money' runs to 30 June 2026 through the MUNIS period-13 ledgers; the town side stops at 30 June 2023, so whether the town's own funds kept growing cannot be said. Measured in /analysis/sitting-on-money. — closes: a MUNIS fund balance report (or trial balance) at period 13 for FY2024, FY2025 and FY2026 covering the town's special revenue funds -- the same system that produced the school delivery of 6 October 2026, pointed at the town's funds.
heldWhether Lunenburg has a written reserve target, and what it isNARROWED 5 October 2026. the Finance Committee files received by records request on 4 October 2026 (sources/budget-workbooks/finance-committee/, see its PROVENANCE note) include a Free Cash Fact Sheet for the FY27 warrant quoting the Town of Lunenburg Free Cash Policy, Section 3.03 (amended 09/02/2014 and 10/18/2018). That is a quotation of the policy, not the adopted policy document, which remains the remedy. Nothing in this archive states a level the town intends to keep in stabilization or free cash — no reserve policy, no fund balance policy, no target as a share of the operating budget. So there is no stated floor any drawdown could be measured against, and "the reserves are healthy" and "the reserves are excessive" are both unfalsifiable here. The Finance Committee has had "Financial Related Policies" as standing Old Business (agenda, 10 September 2026) and funded a financial policies line, so a document may exist or be in progress. — closes: the town’s adopted financial reserve policy, or the Finance Committee’s confirmation in writing that none has been adopted.
heldWhether the Special Education Reserve Fund may be drawn while other special education lines are under their votesMEASURED (/special-education/special-education-overruns): over FY2010-FY2026 at least one of the three special education lines (in district, out-of-district tuition, transportation) ran over its vote in 12 years, but the three together ran over in only 6 -- so in 6 years an overrun on one line sat inside a special education total that came in under. Whether the reserve pays a line's overrun in such a year, or only once money has been moved between lines, decides which series it should be sized against, and the page sizes it on the first, which is OUR choice. The Town Manager's description at the Select Board (7 October 2025) gives the vote needed to spend from the fund and its cap, not the order of draws. A Special Education Reserve Fund Policy is on the Select Board agenda for 27 October 2026. — closes: the Special Education Reserve Fund policy as adopted by the Select Board and the School Committee.
heldWhich cell of DESE’s contribution sheet is mislabelled in FY2020In eighteen of the nineteen differenced years the town’s preliminary contribution equals the previous year’s required contribution multiplied by that year’s municipal revenue growth factor, exactly as DESE’s own User Guide defines it, and the required contribution is that figure adjusted toward target. In FY2020 the two are the other way round: dataContribution!O2593 prints $10,427,328, which is FY2019’s required contribution un-grown, and dataContribution!U2593 prints $10,889,259, which is that figure grown by the 4.43% factor. One of the two cells is carrying the other’s quantity and nothing in the workbook says which. The extract records what the sheet holds rather than repairing it. — closes: DESE’s FY2020 required local contribution worksheet for Lunenburg, which prints the preliminary contribution and the required contribution as separate stated steps.
heldWhy the district and the town state different FY2027 Monty Tech assessmentsMonty Tech’s FY2027 budget presentation puts Lunenburg’s total assessment at $1,452,379, built from a required minimum contribution of $1,378,183 and a transportation and operating assessment of $74,196 with no capital and no bonds. The Town’s own FY2027 operating budget book carries the same line at $1,452,426, in all three of its scenarios. The difference is $47 and neither document acknowledges the other. It is small enough to be a rounding or a late revision and it is not nothing: the two figures are the district’s bill and the town’s appropriation for the same year, and every other year in this archive where both exist ties to the dollar or to eighteen cents. — closes: the district’s FY2027 assessment certification to the Town of Lunenburg, and the Monty Tech line as finally voted at Annual Town Meeting.
moneyAre the printed senior tax work-off totals for the 2018 to 2021 seasons before or after withholding?The reports do not say, while 2022 is printed after withholding and 2024 and 2025 before it, so the totals are not one series. -- closes: the Assessors' commitment of work-off credits for FY2019 to FY2022
moneyDoes FY2024's debt service include the Mass Water Pool 9 balloon payment, or not?The FY2013 annual town report's debt repayment schedule (PDF pages 81-82) prints, in its 2024 column, GRAND TOTAL PRINCIPAL 846,635 and GRAND TOTAL INTEREST 120,310 -- 966,945 -- against a printed TOTAL DEBT of 548,241. The document is out by 418,704 in that one column, and by the same 418,704 in its own TOTAL column (24,298,664 + 7,307,840 = 31,606,504 against a printed 31,187,800). Every other year of the 34 closes exactly. The figures were read off the page's own 400 dpi bitmap twice. 418,704 is also the principal the FY2014 annual report prints for MASS WATER POOL 9 in the FY2024 column -- the only row in that report's 156-row schedule with a principal and NO interest and NO total beside it (sources/data/page-reads/fy2014-p40-debt-schedule.csv). So the discrepancy is located on one borrowing, and it is still not known whether the town excludes that payment from debt service on purpose because the Trust subsidises it, or whether one of the two printed figures is simply wrong. The difference matters: it is 76% of what the town otherwise shows itself owing in FY2024. The per-issue rows of the FY2013 schedule are NOT read -- that limit is already registered as “What does each individual debt issue cost the town in a given year” and is not refiled here. — closes: the Treasurer's debt service schedule for the Mass Water Pollution Abatement Trust loan numbered 9, showing the FY2024 payment and any Trust subsidy against it.
moneyDoes the FY2018 debt repayment schedule's printed grand total account for every issue's INTEREST?IN FY2019 IT DOES NOT, BY THE EXACT INTEREST OF ONE ISSUE. Pages 48-51 of the FY2018 annual town report print sixteen debt issues against FY2019-FY2047 and, separately, GRAND TOTAL rows per year. Read in full, the issues reconcile to those grand totals within $2 in all 29 years -- the schedule shows whole dollars over amounts carrying cents -- except FY2019, where the issues' interest exceeds the printed GRAND TOTAL INTEREST by 272 and TOTAL DEBT by the same 272 while principal ties EXACTLY. 272 is precisely the FY2019 interest of MASS WATER POOL 4, whose own row closes to the dollar (10,409 + 272 = 10,681) and whose 10,409 of principal IS inside the grand total. So one of the two printed figures is wrong and the document does not say which; the archive publishes both and asserts neither. This is the same defect the FY2015 row in this register names for PRINCIPAL, in a different year and a different column, and the two may be worth merging. - closes: the Treasurer's own debt service schedule for FY2019, or the Massachusetts Clean Water Trust (formerly MWPAT) amortization schedule for Pool 4, either of which states that loan's FY2019 interest and admin fee independently of the town's own summary.
moneyDoes the town’s printed debt repayment grand total include all of its debt?IN THE FY2015 REPORT IT DOES NOT, BY THE EXACT AMOUNT OF TWO BONDS. The GRAND TOTAL PRINCIPAL row is short by the two MS-HS CONSTRUCTION bonds in every year column — $625,000 in 2016, $640,000 in 2017, $665,000 in 2018 — while both bonds are printed in the table directly above it. The school construction bonds are the second largest debt on the page. Nothing here establishes whether the row or the table is the intended figure. — closes: the Treasurer’s debt service schedule for FY2015, or the official statement for the MS-HS bonds.
moneyWhat added valuation produced fiscal 2009's $138,168 of new growth?THE ARITHMETIC ON THE PAGE DOES NOT WORK AND FIVE EDITIONS REPRINT IT UNCHANGED. $5,077,276 of added valuation, at the $12.23 rate printed on the same line, gives $62,095 — not the $138,168 beside it. The report’s own percentage-change column corroborates $138,168, so the added-valuation figure is the one that cannot be right. Recorded rather than corrected: which of the two the town meant is not something this archive can say. — closes: DOR’s LA-13 new growth certification for FY2009.
moneyWhat are the $25,276.56 of fines and $3,110.00 of fees that FY2012 receipts counts but does not name?The FY2012 annual town report, PDF p58 (FY 2012 RECEIPTS - JUNE 2012), prints 91 detail lines and a nine-category SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS. The nine categories foot to the printed GRAND TOTAL of $28,471,842.32 exactly; the 91 lines sum to $28,443,455.76, short by $28,386.56. Seven of the nine categories are reproduced to the cent by a partition of those lines, which puts the whole shortfall in two: FINES & FORFEITS, where the page prints only PARKING FINES $2,120.25 and DOG FINES $2,550.00 against a category total of $29,946.81, and FEES, short by $3,110.00. The page was swept end to end and prints no further row, so this is the document omitting detail rather than our reading missing it. Court fines are the obvious candidate for the larger figure and nothing in the report says so. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2012 general ledger revenue detail (MUNIS), which lists every receipt account by code rather than by the summary categories this page prints.
moneyWhat the $600.00 is between the FY2013 receipts page's own detail and its own GRAND TOTALPDF page 63 of the FY2013 annual town report prints FY 2013 RECEIPTS - JUNE 2013: 91 detail lines in three label/amount column-pairs, and beside them a nine-line SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS footing to a printed GRAND TOTAL of $29,744,547.31. The nine summary categories sum to that GRAND TOTAL EXACTLY. The 91 detail lines sum to $29,743,947.31 -- $600.00 less. The reading is not the problem: the page has no text layer and was read off its own 400 dpi bitmap twice, and three of its printed detail blocks foot to their matching summary line to the cent (LICENSES/PERMITS to 174,193.45, STATE REVENUE to 7,010,803.56, FINES & FORFEITS to 27,405.00), which bounds the difference away from 29 of the 91 lines and leaves it inside the fees and departmental revenue lines. The page never states that the detail is exhaustive of the summary, so this is NOT recorded as the town's arithmetic failing -- it may be one receipt listed only in the summary, a line printed $600 low, or two different universes. Nothing on the page distinguishes them. sources/data/page-reads/fy2013-p63-.csv. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2013 year-end revenue report out of the accounting system (the MUNIS revenue ledger for fiscal 2013, which this project already holds for FY2026 as sources/munis-ledgers/revenue/), which lists receipts by account and foots itself.
moneyWhat was Lunenburg's certified assessed valuation and tax rate for fiscal 2021?THREE DOCUMENTS GIVE THREE ANSWERS AND NONE OF THEM IS THE TOWN'S OWN TABLE ADDING UP. The FY2021 annual report, page 38, prints four property classes totalling $1,742,668,758.00 under a Totals line that reads $1,548,256,450 -- and that Totals line, with its $28,054,406.88 levy, is to the cent the one the FY2020 report prints, where it foots FY2020's own four classes at FY2020's rate of 18.12. DLS's assessed-value series puts Lunenburg's FY2021 total at $1,628,643,589, which matches neither. And the rate is printed as 17.19 in every row of the table while the prose above it says the rate went from $18.12 to $17.74 for FY 2021. Until one of these is settled, no FY2021 valuation, levy or rate can be quoted from the annual report, and the class SHARES -- which /commercial-base is built on -- rest on a base the town does not state. The four class rows are internally consistent and are not in doubt: each one's valuation x 17.19 / 1000 is its own printed levy to the cent. — closes: the Division of Local Services Tax Rate Recapitulation (the certified recap, with the LA-4 assessed values) for Lunenburg, fiscal 2021, which DLS publishes per municipality per year on its Gateway/Municipal Databank.
moneyWhat was Lunenburg's certified new growth in fiscal 2012?THE TOWN’S OWN REPORTS GIVE TWO FIGURES AND DISAGREE ABOUT WHICH YEAR EACH BELONGS TO. The FY2013 report prints $19,124,255 against fiscal 2012. The FY2014 through FY2017 reports print $27,729,619 against fiscal 2012 and re-date $19,124,255 to fiscal 2013. Nothing in the archive resolves which labelling is right, and new growth is what the levy limit grows by, so the two readings imply different ceilings. — closes: DOR’s LA-13 new growth certification for FY2012.
moneyWhat was the 2022 senior tax work-off credit before withholding?Only "$7,550.82, after deductions" is printed, and the report's $15 rate is the rate when it was written, not the rate paid in 2022. -- closes: the 2022 payroll register for the program
moneyWhat was the market value of each trust fund, the Stabilization Fund among them, at 30 June 2007?report-trust-funds carries an ENDING MARKET VALUE column in the 2010 report (and the FY-era trust tables). The 2007 trust fund pages (PDF pages 74-75) print only FY 07 ENDING CASH VALUE, with a REALIZED G/L FY 07 column and no unrealized gain or market value: the text was searched for market value and unrealized, and the only hits are bank money-market accounts on the treasurer's cash page (p73). — closes: the Treasurer's or custodian's 30 June 2007 trust fund statements at market value.
moneyWhat was the total senior tax work-off credit for the 2015 and 2017 seasons?The annual reports print hours and a $10 rate, not a total; hours times the rate is our ceiling, not a printed figure. -- closes: the Assessors' FY2016 and FY2018 totals of work-off credits
moneyWhat were Lunenburg’s fiscal 2011 class valuations, where the town’s own two printings disagree by $7,295,100?The FY2011 annual town report prints the same quantity twice on one page (PDF p12, printed folio 9) and the two do not reconcile. Fiscal 2011 Assessments and Revenues by Major Property Class puts Commercial at 64,514,700 and foots its tax levy to the printed 18,006,811.48 to the cent; the Fiscal Year 2011 Abstract of Assessments below it puts 300 - 393 Commercial at 56,208,300 and 600 - 821 Chapter 61, 61A, 61B at 1,011,300, so its twelve classes sum to 1,106,987,789 against its own printed TOTALS of 1,114,282,889. The residual is 7,295,100 and it sits entirely in the commercial class: the abstract’s eight residential lines sum to 1,000,004,500, which is the first table’s Residential valuation to the dollar, and its account count ties exactly at 5,185, so no row is missing from the reading. Both cells were re-read off the page’s own 400 dpi bitmap at 6x. Which printing is wrong is not established, and the report itself settles nothing — the first table’s own TOTALS cell is misprinted 1,114,2828,889, ten digits. — closes: the Assessors’ certified fiscal 2011 Tax Recapitulation (DOR Form LA-4/LA-5) for Lunenburg, which states valuation by class as the Department of Revenue certified it and is the only document that outranks both printings.
moneyWhich account pays for senior tax work-off credits: the overlay, or an appropriation?The Assessors' minutes say it "likely comes out of overlay" (4 September 2024) and record a member asking the question (4 February 2026); neither states it. -- closes: the Town Accountant's year-end overlay reconciliation showing the work-off charges
moneyWhich figure is wrong in the FY2013 Omnibus Budget: the eleven section totals, or the $600 larger Total Omnibus?The budget Town Meeting voted under Article 8 is printed in the FY2012 annual town report, PDF pp.81-82. Every one of its eleven sections foots to its own printed subtotal exactly, and those eleven subtotals sum to $27,488,841.00 against a printed Total Omnibus of $27,489,441.00 — six hundred dollars more. Both figures were re-read upright at full scale off the page's own 518 dpi bitmap, so this is the document disagreeing with itself and not a misreading. The $600 could be a line the page does not print, a section total understated, or the grand total overstated, and nothing on those two pages distinguishes them. — closes: the Town Clerk's certified copy of the Article 8 motion and the FY2013 budget handouts it refers to (Refer to Handouts on pages 27 – 30), which the annual report does not reproduce.
moneyWhich total is right for the 2012 and 2024 senior tax work-off seasons?Two town sources disagree: $9,520.00 against two approvals adding to $8,720.00 for 2012, and $9,607.50 against $9,674.50 for 2024. -- closes: the Assessors' list of work-off credits for FY2013 and FY2025
moneyWhose $92,709.54 is the unnamed line in the FY2015 receivables summary?THE REPORT PRINTS A FIGURE ON A LINE WITH NO NAME. $92,709.54 in the PAYMENTS column, under UTILITY LIENS ADDED TO TAXES, with an empty name cell — confirmed by rendering page 45 rather than off the scan. Seven of the eight columns tie to the cent without it and PAYMENTS is short by exactly that amount, so the figure is real and the name is what is missing. Carried in the data as (the page prints no name for this line). — closes: the Collector’s detail behind the FY2015 receivables summary.
moneyWhy does the same $1,085,674.86 appear twice in the town’s FY2015 opening receivables?THE TOWN’S OWN TWO BOOKS DO NOT MEET, AND THE AMOUNT IS EXACT. FY2014 closes MEADOW BETTERMENT at $1,085,674.86. FY2015 opens SEWER BETTERMENT $1,085,674.86 higher than FY2014 closed it, AND carries the same $1,085,674.86 again on a new MEADOW WOODS WATER BETT line. Both years tie to their own printed GRAND TOTAL, and line by line every other balance rolls forward near-exactly. A recoding of Meadow Woods into the sewer betterment line would explain it; so would a restatement; nothing published distinguishes them. — closes: the town’s FY2015 receivable roll-forward, or the MUNIS receivable detail for both years.
moneyWhy does the town open FY2018 owed $13,300 more than it closed FY2017 owing?THE TOWN PRINTS BOTH FIGURES AND THEY DO NOT MEET. A receivable balance rolls forward: what the town was owed on 30 June is what it starts the next year owed. Every other consecutive pair we can read ties to the cent (FY2020 through FY2024, one pair off by 2c). The Collector’s grand total on FY2017 page 45 reads $9,008,228.35 and on FY2018 page 54 reads $9,021,528.35 — checked on the pages, not off our extract. A prior-year adjustment, a reclassified charge and a typo all fit it equally and nothing published distinguishes them. — closes: the Collector’s receivable control reconciliation for FY2018, which is a report the accounting system can print.
money_inBus feescharged by published policy · no destination found in any ledger
money_inGrants received in earlier yearsspent now, booked then · nine funds, no FY26 revenue
money_inHow do Ipswich, Woburn, Lenox, Medford, Canton, Norwood fund schools in the top quarter of spending while taxing homes in the lightest quarter?Of the 20 towns that spend among the most per pupil while asking the least of a home’s value, 6 fit none of the four routes this report can test: an unusual amount of state aid, many houses per child, houses worth a great deal each, or an unusually large business base. Three of them — Woburn, Canton, Norwood — carry business shares of roughly twice the median and fail only the exact 2x test. Whatever the rest are doing is the most directly useful thing on this page and nothing here identifies it. — closes: DLS Schedule A for each town, which reports every revenue source a municipality collects, so local receipts, enterprise funds and reserves can be compared rather than inferred.
money_inHow many Montachusett foundation-enrolment students did Harvard have in FY2018 — 7 or 8?The FY2017 annual town report prints the figure twice and the two disagree by one student. Page 144 is DESE's own FY18 Chapter 70 / Regional District Enrollment and Contributions by Member City or Town for LEA 832 and prints HARVARD at 7; page 148 is the district's COMMUNITY ASSESSMENTS table and prints its FOUNDATION ENROLLMENT at 8. The two agree on all 17 other towns and on all 18 Required Minimum Contributions to the dollar. Only page 148's column foots to the District Total of 1,496 that BOTH pages print; page 144's 18 rows sum to 1,495, although its own per-row Change identities all close. Foundation enrolment is the input Chapter 70 runs on, so a member town's count is load-bearing for every town's assessment — and neither page says which of its own figures is the error. — closes: DESE's published FY18 Chapter 70 regional district enrolment file for LEA 832 Montachusett, at doe.mass.edu, which is the source both pages reproduce.
money_inHow many weighing and measuring devices did Lunenburg's Sealer test and seal in 2003?report-weights-measures holds the Sealer's device counts and fees charged (2010 p24-p25). The 2003 annual town report prints no Sealer's report: its Textract text was searched for devices, scales, sealed, sealing, condemned, adjusted, savings impact and Chapter 295, and returned the appointment (p8), SEALING FEES $401.00 in receipts (p52), the appropriation line (p55) and the bylaw fee schedule voted at ATM Article 24 (p89-p90), which is a rate, not a count (sources/data/report-tables/2003/). — closes: the Sealer of Weights and Measures' 2003 annual report to the Division of Standards.
money_inHow many weighing and measuring devices did the Sealer test in 1959, and what did sealing bring in by device?report-weights-measures holds the Sealer's device counts and report-fee-schedule the fee per device from the 2001-2010 reports. The 1959 report gives the year's total in prose on p42-43 (One hundred and seventy weighing and measuring devices were adjusted and sealed, a net cost to the Town of $427.22) and the Treasurer's receipts one line, Sealer's Fees $98.50 (p21), with no count or fee by device type. Searched sealer and weights and measures (sources/data/report-tables/1959/). — closes: the Sealer of Weights and Measures' 1959 test and fee record.
money_inHow many weighing and measuring devices did the Sealer test in 1960, and what did sealing bring in by device?report-weights-measures holds the Sealer's device counts and sealing-fee-schedule the fee per device from the 2001-2010 reports. The 1960 report gives the year's total in prose (p43: one hundred sixty-seven devices adjusted and sealed) and the fees collected as one receipt line (p21: Sealer's Fees $94.60); no count or fee by type of device (searched p5, 21, 22, 29, 43, 59, 119) — closes: the Sealer's annual return to the Division of Standards
money_inHow many weighing and measuring devices did the Sealer test in 1961, and what did sealing bring in by device?report-weights-measures and report-fee-schedule read the Sealer's counts and fees from the 2003-2004 reports. The 1961 report prints the Sealer's page as prose only (p51): 163 devices adjusted and sealed and a net cost to the Town of $524.12, no count by device type and no fee by device; the Treasurer's receipts show Sealer's Fees 92.20 (p25). Searched sealer, weights and measures (sources/data/report-tables/1961/). — closes: the Inspector of Weights and Measures' 1961 test and fee record.
money_inHow many weighing and measuring devices did the Sealer test in 1962, and what did sealing bring in by device?report-weights-measures holds device counts from the 2001-2010 reports. The 1962 report gives one sentence (p45: One hundred sixty weighing and measuring devices were adjusted and sealed during 1962, net cost to the Town $428.09) and the Treasurer's receipt line Sealer's Fees $93.10 (p20), with no count or fee by device type; searched weights and measures, sealer, devices (sources/data/report-tables/1962/). — closes: the Sealer of Weights and Measures' 1962 test and fee record.
money_inHow many weighing and measuring devices did the Sealer test in 1963, and what did sealing bring in by device type?report-weights-measures holds the Sealer's device counts and sealing-fee-schedule the fee per device from the 2001-2010 reports. The 1963 report gives the year's totals in prose on p48 (160 devices inspected, 155 adjusted and sealed, 5 condemned) and the Treasurer's receipts one line, Sealer's Fees $92.10 (p22), and the Sealer's budget line (p24); no count or fee by device type. Searched weights (p5, p24, p31, p48, p65) (sources/data/report-tables/1963/). — closes: the Sealer of Weights and Measures' 1963 test and fee record.
money_inHow many weighing and measuring devices did the Sealer test in 1964, and what did sealing bring in by device?report-weights-measures holds the Sealer's activity from later reports. 1964 prints the Sealer's narrative (p46, about the State-owned standards) and sealing fees received ($96.80, p20 receipts), with no count or fee by device type. Searched sealer, weights and measures, sealing (pages 5, 20, 22, 28, 46, 63, 122) (sources/data/report-tables/1964/). — closes: the Inspector of Weights and Measures' 1964 test and fee record.
money_inHow many weighing and measuring devices did the Sealer test in 1965, and what did sealing bring in by device?report-weights-measures holds the Sealer's device counts and fee schedule from the 2001-2010 reports. money_inHow much of Monty Tech’s FY2026 spending is outside its operating budget, and from which fundsThe district’s FY 2027 Budget Summary sets out its operating (general fund) budget for FY2026 and FY2027 and the five sources that pay for it: Chapter 70, the member towns’ assessments, state transportation aid, its Regional Transportation Fund and its Excess & Deficiency reserve. Grants and revolving funds are not in it. DESE’s expenditures-by-function file DOES split the district’s total by fund, general fund against grants and revolving, but only through FY2025, and that total, which DESE titles Expenditure (Admin, Instruction, Operations), carries no capital or debt service row. So the operating budget on /enrolment/monty-tech-funding and DESE’s per-pupil figure are different years and different scopes, and nothing here reconciles them. — closes: DESE’s End of Year Financial Report for LEA 08320000 for FY2026, which splits spending by fund.
money_inHow much of free cash is the schools’Free cash is certified for the town as a whole. Neither the DLS proof nor the Town’s own undesignated fund balance roll-forward attributes any component to any department, so nothing published says how much of it the school department’s unspent appropriation produced — nor how much of any appropriation of it reaches the schools. The projection on this site is built from budget columns and free cash is derived from actuals; they are subtracted once, side by side, and never joined. — closes: a departmental turnback schedule for the year-end close, which would split the unexpended appropriations line by department.
money_inHow much of the After School Activities fund's income is the student activity fee, and how much is families paying for one named trip, exam or prom?MEASURED in the school journal, FY2023-FY2026: the fund's income accounts are titled ACTIVITY FEES by school, and some deposits go in under a memo naming Nature's Classroom, a test or a prom (the amount is computed on the page below); most name only the school. Deposits are posted in batches, so the journal cannot split them. The School Committee's $70 student activity fee may not be deposited here at all: the district also keeps student activity accounts outside the Town's books, and its payment portal sells an Afterschool Activity Fee and Field Trips separately. Shown on /school-all-funds/activities-fund. — closes: the deposit detail behind each batch, by activity, and which account the student activity fee is paid into.
money_inHow much of the FY2027 enacted state-aid increase is receipts and how much is offsetting assessmentsmodel/finance.py grows a FY2027 base of $11,404,917 + $471,121. The first is the Governor’s GROSS cherry sheet Total Receipts, printed by the FY2027 Town Meeting booklet. The second is recorded in fy27-and-the-override.md as NET — "+$471,121 net (Ch.70, charter/choice receiving tuition, Smart Growth, UGGA, vets/elderly exemptions; offset by higher charter assessments)". A gross figure and a net figure are being added, so the gross FY2027 receipt estimate the projection actually grows is not established, and neither is how much of the increase the Town keeps. This archive holds no Cherry Sheet for any year, which is the only document that prints receipts and assessments side by side. — closes: the FY2027 Cherry Sheet for Lunenburg on the enacted budget (DLS form CS 1-ER), which states each receipt and each assessment separately.
money_inHow much of the SY2025 grant fall was ESSER, as against every other grant and revolving fundThe meeting record names ESSER as the cause repeatedly and with figures — the district told the School Committee on 15 November 2023 “We have a loss of $650,000 in ESSER funds, this is much more significant than we expected”, and on 17 January 2024 put the loss at $600,000 beside a $500,000 health insurance rise. DESE reports one combined grants_revolving column, which holds ESSER, Title I and the other federal and state grants together with circuit breaker, school choice, athletics, food service and every other revolving fund. The SY2025 fall of $2,023,188 across matched functions therefore cannot be attributed to any one of them. The district's own stated ESSER figures and this fall are different quantities measured at different stages — a forward budget gap against a closed-year fund total — and this project does not difference one against the other. — closes: the district's end-of-year grant expenditure detail by grant code for FY2024 and FY2025, or Schedule 19 of its End of Year Financial Report as filed, which lists each grant separately.
money_inHow much of the federal grant money Monty Tech is allocated serves Lunenburg studentsDESE allocates Perkins, IDEA and the Title grants to Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical as one district, and it serves students from every member town (/school-all-funds/grants-others-receive). Lunenburg gets no Perkins allocation of its own, and nothing published says what part of Monty Tech's serves Lunenburg's students. — closes: Monty Tech's grant applications and budgets, by programme and by member town
money_inHow much of the special education circuit breaker account's balance is already committed to the next year's tuition?The account (fund 2640) pays out-of-district tuition every year, overrun or not, and its 30 June balance is computed on /analysis/special-education-costs and /analysis/sitting-on-money. Whether that balance is free to meet a mid-year surprise, or is already planned against next year's placements, is not published: the year-end ledgers show what was spent, not what was intended, and in one year the account carried a tuition budget while in the others it carried none. So a resident cannot tell how much of the balance is a cushion beside the new special education reserve. — closes: the district's circuit breaker spending plan for the year, or the budget narrative for the out-of-district tuition line stating how much it assumes the account will pay.
money_inHow the $1,500 athletic family cap was arrived at, and over what periodThe School Committee minutes of 26 February 2025 record the decision and not the derivation: "A slideshow presentation of athletic user fees is presented ... with a family cap of $1500. ... all approve via roll call vote". A slideshow WAS presented, so the arithmetic exists somewhere; this archive does not hold it, and the only athletics presentation material here is two Athletic Advisory Council agendas from the preceding weeks. Minutes summarise, so the absence of arithmetic in them is not evidence that there was none — what is established is that no document we hold derives the figure or states the period it covers. The figure itself is unreachable per season by family size alone: five children at one sport each come to between $1,220 and $1,375 depending on how the sibling discount is carried past the third child, both under $1,500. — closes: the athletic user fee presentation given to the School Committee on 26 February 2025, which is the slideshow the minutes name.
money_inHow was the 1963 tax rate of $82.00 built up from the levy, overlay and estimated receipts (the Assessors' recapitulation)?The recapitulation form is printed on p9 and explained on p8, but Textract returned every amount split into digit groups across cells, so no figure was landed (NEEDS.md item 1); report-valuation holds the equivalent from the 1987-2010 reports. The prose gives some of it: Item E gross amount to be raised $1,572,964.98, motor vehicle excise $142,661.61 of $459,887.39 estimated receipts, net to be raised $921,071.25 (p8). The overlay of $29,000.00 and the 1962 deficit are on p9 only. — closes: a re-read of the p9 form in digit-group-aware form (the page is in the archive); the filed Tax Recap sheet itself.
money_inStudent activity accountsheld by the school under its own authority · not in the town’s books at all
money_inTrust fund incomescholarships, cemetery, stabilisation · extract is check-failed
money_inWhat Chapter 70 aid would actually do if enrollment fellMUCH NARROWER THAN IT WAS. DESE’s Chapter 70 trends workbook breaks the aid calculation into its named components, and for Lunenburg they show that this year’s aid is last year’s aid plus named increments — an identity that holds to the dollar in every one of the last seven years. In FY2026 the whole of the increase is the minimum aid increment, $240,450, which is exactly $150.00 for each of the 1,603 foundation pupils, and the foundation aid increment is zero. Over thirty-four years foundation enrollment fell in 17 and aid fell in 3 — FY1997, FY2010 and FY2011. DESE’s component columns show a reduction applied in FY2010 and FY2011; they start at FY2007, so nothing in this archive says why aid fell in FY1997. So the marginal aid attached to one foundation pupil is currently about $150 and not the $14,440 foundation budget per pupil. What is NOT established: that the Legislature sets the same minimum aid rate next year — it has ranged from $30 to $150 a pupil in the years published — nor what happens if a large enough enrollment fall moves the district off the minimum aid track, which no document here models. — closes: DESE’s preliminary Chapter 70 aid calculation for Lunenburg for the year in question, which states the foundation aid, minimum aid and hold-harmless components before the year is set.
money_inWhat FY2027 athletic fees are for anyone other than a full-paying high school familyThe only account this archive has of the 2026-27 athletic fees is a Superintendent’s email to families in August 2026 that we do not hold, reported as four figures: a first, second and third child and a family cap. FY2026 published more than that — a middle school rate, a reduced rate for high school and for middle school, and a sibling discount — and none of those has an FY2027 successor in any document here. So a middle school family, a family paying the reduced fee and a family whose fee is waived cannot be priced for the year now running. — closes: the district’s athletic fee schedule as published to families for 2026-27, in full, including the reduced and waived rates and the middle school schedule.
money_inWhat Lunenburg receives for a child who chooses IN, and what the fall from 51 to 15 is worthDESE counts the children arriving in Lunenburg from other towns in every school year from SY2014 to SY2026: 51 at the start, 15 at the end, a fall of 71% while the number leaving stayed flat. The town’s own School Choice fund receipts fell over the ten years the two series share, from $220,058 in FY2014 to $116,976 in FY2023. Neither document states a RATE. The statutory base tuition is set by M.G.L. c.76 §12B, no document in this archive states it, and it is higher for special education; the arriving children also come by three different mechanisms — school choice, tuition waived by local agreement, and foster placement — which do not carry money the same way. So the two series can be published side by side and cannot be divided into each other: a per-student figure produced that way would be an assumption in a measurement’s clothes, and the money value of a 71% fall in arrivals is therefore not established anywhere on this site. — closes: the DLS Cherry Sheet CS 1-ER (estimated receipts) for Lunenburg, which prints School Choice Receiving Tuition as its own receipt line, for the years the DESE counts cover.
money_inWhat Monty Tech’s tuition, payments from other school systems and miscellaneous local revenue were forThe Census Bureau’s FY2024 school finance survey reports three large local items for Monty Tech that are neither its member towns’ assessments nor private gifts: tuition from pupils, parents and private sources (item A07), payments from other school systems for tuition, transportation and other services (D11), and refunds and other local revenue (U97). The amounts are on /monty-tech/monty-tech-revenue, item by item. The survey names each item and says nothing about what produced it. Monty Tech’s FY2024 budget book lists Practical Nursing and Continuing and Post Graduate Studies staff among those paid from revolving or special-revenue funds, so programmes that could charge tuition exist; it prints no revenue for them, and its general-fund revenue table budgets nothing for miscellaneous receipts or interest. So whether A07 is adult and practical-nursing tuition, whether D11 is tuition for out-of-district pupils, and what U97 holds are hypotheses nothing here tests. — closes: Monty Tech’s audited financial statements for FY2024, which report revenue by fund, and its revenue detail by account for the same year.
money_inWhat Parks & Recreation’s programme fees and beach-pass sales became on the town’s books — how much of the $38,955.50 of programme fees and $8,828.00 of passes MyRec recorded for FY2025 reached fund 1500 (Park Revolving) or the general fund, and whenMyRec is the registration system, not the ledger: its FY2025 sales reports foot to their own totals but say nothing about deposits, refunds or the fund each fee was posted to, and the FY2025 special-revenue report is not in the archive — closes: the FY2025 special-revenue report and the journal detail for fund 1500, the same report the archive holds for fund 1301.
money_inWhat a family spends in the cafeteria when the standard meal is freeMassachusetts funds universal free school meals and the district takes the programme, so the standard reimbursable meal is not billed to a household — that much is established and it is a real reduction in what families pay. What is outside the programme is not: a la carte items, snacks and second meals are charged, and no price list for them is held here. The School Lunch fund’s own revenue cannot separate the two. — closes: the district’s cafeteria a la carte price list for 2026-27.
money_inWhat a fourth child in one family pays for high school athleticsThe FY2027 schedule names a first, second and third child — $400, $300 and $225 — and stops. The FY2024 and FY2025 schedules did the same, and there the cap resolved it: the three published rates sum to exactly the $475 the FAQ prints as the cap, so a fourth child added nothing. That identity does not hold in FY2027, where the three rates sum to $925 against a $1,500 cap, so the fourth child is neither priced nor obviously free. A family of four children — the case residents ask about most often — therefore cannot be costed from anything published. — closes: the district’s athletic fee schedule as published to families for 2026-27, stating the rate for each additional child or the point at which the ladder stops.

Whether the tier was dropped or simply omitted from the email is not established, and the difference decides whether a qualifying single-child household pays $50, $180, or nothing. — closes: the adopted transportation fee schedule for 2026-27, with every tier and the free/reduced provision, as approved by the School Committee.

money_inWhat did each of the ~130 individual receipt lines on the FY2019 receipts page bring in?PDF page 30 of the FY2019 annual town report (printed folio 28), FY 2019 RECEIPTS - JUNE 2019, prints about 130 named receipt lines in three label/amount column pairs, and separately a nine-category SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS with a GRAND TOTAL. The SUMMARY is now read and closes to the printed GRAND TOTAL of $40,734,004.07 to the cent (sources/data/page-reads/fy2019-p30-receipts.csv). THE DETAIL IS NOT READ. The page is a ~150 dpi photograph with no text layer, and recognition finds only about 75 of the ~130 printed money figures, so the second identity the page states about itself -- that the detail lines also sum to the GRAND TOTAL -- is untested. money_inWhat part of Lunenburg’s Monty Tech assessment the property tax levy pays, rather than state aid or other receiptsA member town pays its regional assessment out of one budget that the levy, Chapter 70 and local receipts fund together, and no document assigns one revenue to one appropriation. For the other seventeen member towns only the state-required minimum is held, not the whole assessment. — closes: nothing assigns it; the town’s tax recapitulation sheet sets every appropriation against the levy and every receipt, and each member town’s voted Monty Tech appropriation would replace the minimum.
money_inWhat period the school athletic family cap coversThe $1,500 family cap was set by the School Committee on 26 February 2025 and the minutes state the amount and no period: "with a family cap of $1500". The cap it replaced did state one — the LHS Athletics FAQ prints "Total Cap per season=$475.00" — so the schedule has moved from a stated period to none. The district workbook obtained by records request carries the per-student rates on three worksheets named for the three seasons and carries no family cap in any cell, so the corroboration that dates the other rates does not reach this one. Read per season and read per year, $1,500 is a different bill for the same family. The arithmetic argues for the annual reading — with the published FY2027 ladder a family of five children playing one sport each in one season reaches $1,375, still under the cap — but that is an inference from the cap being unreachable, not a statement in any document. — closes: the district’s athletic fee schedule as published to families for 2026-27, which is the document the Superintendent’s August 2026 email to families attached or described.
money_inWhat put $62,231 into the School Facilities Use fund (1306) in FY2025 — the balance went from $3,010.67 at 30 June 2024 to $65,241.82 at 30 June 2025, more than the fund has taken in in any of the thirteen years the annual reports printRent alone cannot produce the rise: the best receipts year on record is $39,944. Either revenue arrived that is not field rent — a transfer, a reimbursement, an insurance recovery — or something that had been charged to the fund stopped being charged to it, and the two balances cannot tell those apart. FY2025 is the one year no special-revenue schedule is published for. THE TEST WHEN THE DATA ARRIVES: read FY2025 line by line, total the receipts that are field or building rent, and see whether the remainder is a transfer in or an expenditure that moved elsewhere — closes: the journal detail for fund 1306, FY2024–FY2026, and the FY2025 special-revenue report.
money_inWhat quantity the Town’s own published state-aid growth rates of 5.3% and 1.4% measureThe FY2027 Town Meeting booklet states that "From FY13-FY23 state aid increased at an annual rate of 5.3%, but in the last four years, it has slowed to approximately 1.4%" (3765-town-meeting-booklet-including-warrant, line 338), and does not say which figure it grew. Rebuilding the Town’s own Subtotal State Aid line from its own revenue/expenditure worksheets — 23 consecutive budget years, FY2005 to FY2027, notes/findings/state-aid-budget-series.csv — gives 4.5660% for FY2013→FY2023 and 1.9144% for FY2023→FY2027. Neither published rate is reproducible from the Town’s own published series, so a rate quoted to Town Meeting cannot be checked against anything. — closes: the Cherry Sheets themselves (DLS form CS 1-ER for Lunenburg, one per year), or the Town Manager’s working file behind the FY2027 booklet’s revenue narrative.
money_inWhat the athletic fee fund held at each 30 June, FY2021 to FY2026SETTLED IN PART, 28 October 2026. They are not one basis. The FY2025 figure is the fund's cash -- the cashbook closes FY2025 at the same cent -- and is $20,991.20 above the $110,247.89 fund balance the district file opens FY2026 with; that file calls the gap accounts payable but dates it 6/30/26, while the journal shows it paid on 8 July 2025. By our running total of the cashbook, the fund's cash went below zero inside FY2024 and FY2025 (lowest -$117,947.62, 21 March 2025) before journal entries moved costs onto the town budget. Shown on /athletics/fee-fund-history. — closes: the Town Accountant's fund 1301 balance sheet at 30 June 2024, 2025 and 2026 (the MUNIS balance sheet report, period 13), showing cash, accounts payable and fund balance separately.
money_inWhat the foundation budget pays per pupil for each kind of childDESE builds the foundation budget from per-pupil rates that differ by grade and by category, and it publishes the CATEGORIES for Lunenburg — FY2026 foundation enrollment of 1,603, of whom 54 are English learners (3.4%), 452 are low income (28.8%, low-income group 5) and none is vocational, at a wage adjustment factor of 1.000 — without publishing the rate attached to any of them in the same file. money_inWhat the processing fee is on every school payment made onlineThe Superintendent’s email of 17 August 2026 tells families paying online that "RevTrak charges a small processing fee" and does not say what it is. It is added to every other fee a family pays through the portal, so it scales with the rest of the bill rather than sitting beside it, and a household paying athletics, bus and activity fees online pays it three times. "Small" is not a rate. — closes: the RevTrak merchant agreement or the portal’s own fee disclosure, stating whether the charge is a percentage, a flat amount per transaction, or both.
money_inWhat the six fees the district’s payment portal sells actually costThe district’s RevTrak portal offers an Afterschool Activity Fee, a Chromebook Repair Fee, Extended Day & ELC, Field Trips, an LHS Parking Permit and a Primary Preschool Program. So the existence of each fee is established and the amount of every one of them is not, and any total of what a Lunenburg family pays the schools in a year is a floor with six named items sitting above it. — closes: the district’s published schedule of student fees for the current year, listing every fee the portal charges with its amount.

money_inWhat was the Town owed in motor vehicle excise, user charges and betterments at 30 June 2016?THE FY2016 RECEIVABLES SUMMARY IS PRINTED CLIPPED, AND THE CLOSING COLUMNS ARE THE ONES CUT OFF. Page 47 of the FY2016 annual town report prints the property-tax half of the schedule with EIGHT columns -- FORWARD, COMMITTMENTS, ADJUSTMENTS, REFUNDS, PAYMENTS, ABATEMENTS, TRANSFER, BALANCES -- and every row closes on the identity those columns state. Page 48 (motor vehicle excise, twenty levy years) stops after PAYMENTS. Page 49 (deferred taxes, water and sewer user charges, utility liens, sewer/water/street/septic betterments, apportioned assessments) stops after REFUNDS, and its own title is cut mid-word -- FY2016 COLLECTION OF TAXE. Page 50 is blank but for its folio, so nothing continues. Both pages were rendered and looked at on 2 October 2026: the ruled table simply ends at the right-hand edge of the page. SO THERE IS NO PUBLISHED BALANCE for any of those accounts and no arithmetic on either page can be closed. The combined balance sheet on page 20 does not substitute: it prints one undivided EXCISES $243,852.65 against page 48's five columns netting $303,306.05, which are not the same quantity. This is NOT the same gap as the FY2013/FY2017/FY2020 receivables refusals, which are about an extractor failing on pages that ARE fully printed -- here the document does not carry the figures. — closes: the Collector's and Treasurer's own FY2016 receivables control report, or an un-clipped printing of the same worksheet, which the Town Accountant's system can reproduce.
