money_inWhat was the balance on 1 July 2022, and so on each 30 June since, of the 27 school funds that neither the FY2023 annual town report's special revenue schedule nor the Town's 31 March 2026 special revenue ledger lists?sources/data/school-fund-flows.csv carries what each of these funds received and spent in FY2023-FY2026, from the journal, but no opening balance, so no balance: the capital articles (3105, 3109, 3111, 3112, 3118, 3119, 3123), the 42xx FY2026 grants (4201-4206), the scholarships (8130, 8134), grants opened after FY2023 (2668, 2688, 2689, 2707, 2759, 2839, 2844, 2845, 2868, 2962), and two town-wide funds the school journal holds only part of (2583 Green Communities, 2595 ARPA). For a fund opened during the run the opening is probably zero, but nothing printed says so, and a capital article's balance sits outside the special revenue schedule altogether. — closes: the Town Accountant's balance sheet by fund (MUNIS fund balance or trial balance) at 30 June 2022, for every fund that holds a school account.
money_inWhat would regionalising actually be worth to Lunenburg, once the transport reimbursement is set against the transport costs it would also take on?NARROWED 26 September 2026, and half of it is now answered. The reimbursement side is measured: the DLS Cherry Sheet is in the archive, FY2010–FY2027, and Regional Transportation under M.G.L. c.71 s.16C is $88,183,608 statewide in FY2026 to 84 regional districts and nothing to any single-town district. North Middlesex draws $1,195,321, Ashburnham-Westminster $1,190,725, Groton-Dunstable $1,001,384. What is NOT answerable from any file is the other half: a regional district also INCURS the busing it is reimbursed for, and no published figure separates a district’s transport cost from its reimbursement — DESE’s twelve per-pupil categories carry no transport line at all. Nor is the counterfactual observable: what three towns would spend merged is not what other merged towns spend today. — closes: the regional districts’ own budgets, which state transportation as a line and the reimbursement against it; and a regional agreement, which sets how the net cost is apportioned.
money_inWhere did the Town's other receipts and payments come from, as a share, in the 1964 Where Did Your 1964 Tax Dollar Go? chart?p14 prints a pie of the tax dollar by service in cents (schools 73.2 cents, and slices a-f) and p15 a receipts and payments analysis; Textract read the large slices as page lines only (p14 has no table cells, p15 only the small slices a-i), so the large slices are not in report-expenditure-shares as cells. Searched pages 13-15 lines and cells (sources/data/report-tables/1964/). — closes: a readable copy of the p14-15 charts, or the Treasurer's chart workpaper.
money_inWhere did the rest of the FY2026 circuit breaker payment go?DESE's reimbursement file lists $579,142 paid to Lunenburg in FY2026. The school circuit breaker fund (2640) booked $325,970 in FY2026, but $40,966 of that is FY2025's supplemental payment, posted in July 2025; FY2026's own payments booked are two installments of $142,502 (September and December 2025), $285,004. The other $294,138 -- the spring and June installments -- is not in fund 2640 through period 13. It may be booked in a later year, as $100,377 of FY2024's payment was in FY2025, or to another fund; the school ledger cannot say which. (Corrected 26 October 2026 from $253,172, which netted the FY2025 supplemental against FY2026.) It bears on the tuition vote, which since FY2025 counts on the repayment in advance (/special-education/circuit-breaker). Searched 26 October 2026: every school fund in the journal through 30 June 2026 (nothing after December), and the Town general fund revenue report to 31 March 2026, whose only special education line is SPED REIMB, $61,499.11 -- too early to hold a spring installment, and not shaped like one. -- closes: the same Town general fund revenue report (glytdbud) run for FY2026 period 13, or the Treasurer's cash receipts for the FY2026 circuit breaker payments, by date and the fund each was credited to
money_inWhere do the other towns’ ski co-op reimbursements land when they are paid?Lunenburg bills Littleton, Narragansett and Leominster for their skiers’ shares — $9,736.57 for 2025-26 — and which account receives the money decides whether it offsets the athletics line, the athletic revolving fund, or general revenue. The invoice is a bill and does not show receipt — closes: the revenue detail for the account the checks are deposited to, or the athletic revolving fund cashbook for the season
money_inWhere the PEG Access balance went between FY2019 and FY2021The fund's carried balance is continuous in the report from FY2015 to FY2019 -- each edition's Starting Balance is the previous edition's Ending Balance to the cent -- and then stops being a series. FY2019 prints a Total of $573,837.37 (starting balance, plus revenue, less expenses, plus the Comcast Tech Fund of $124,796.01); FY2020 opens at $447,813.36, $126,024.01 lower; FY2021 opens at $272,000.00, which the same page's prose states is the budget rather than a balance. One document explains part of it: Article 16 of the FY2019 Annual Town Meeting established a PEG Access Enterprise Fund under MGL c.44 s53F1/2 and transferred into it the balances of the PEG Access and Cable Related Receipts Reserved For Appropriation Fund and the Comcast Tech Capital Grant Fund as of 30 June 2019. So the fund changed legal form at exactly this point, which is why the statement changes shape. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: the amounts transferred, and therefore whether the $126,024.01 step is the transfer, a closing entry, a restatement, or something else. There is also a smaller unexplained step earlier, FY2017's Ending Balance $303,909.77 against FY2018's Starting Balance $303,551.54, $358.23 apart, with no fund change to account for it. -- closes: the Town Accountant's opening and closing trial balances for the PEG Access and Cable Related funds for FY2018, FY2019 and FY2020, showing the transfers in and out.
money_inWhether Lunenburg receives Title III English-learner money through a consortiumMEASURED (/school-all-funds/grants-others-receive): most of Lunenburg's comparison districts are allocated Title III; Lunenburg is on none of DESE's Title III allocation pages, FY2017-FY2027. DESE allocates Title III only where a district's amount reaches the statutory floor, and at the median rate per learner our estimate puts Lunenburg just under it. A district under the floor can join a consortium, and DESE's pages do not list a consortium's members. — closes: DESE's Title III consortium membership list for each year, or the district's Title III application.
money_inWhether Lunenburg’s free cash is unusual for a town its sizeThe DLS proof carries no denominator — no population, budget, revenue or levy for any of the nine towns, Lunenburg included. So Littleton’s $11.3M against Shirley’s $272K says nothing about which is closer to its own target, and free cash as a share of the operating budget cannot be computed for a peer at all. Composition and volatility are ratios and do compare; the level does not, and is not shown. — closes: the Tax Rate Recapitulation (Schedule A) for each town, which prints the operating budget the ratio needs.
money_inWhether a shortfall in state aid falls on the schools or on the rest of the townChapter 70 is 35% of the school appropriation and the town has no vote on it, so which side of the budget absorbs a miss is the question a resident actually has. Nothing published answers it. The free cash proof states one net cherry sheet figure for the whole town; the general ledger’s state aid accounts share no organisation code with any expense account, 0 of 222, so no aid dollar can be followed to anything it paid for; and the appropriation is voted before the final aid number is known. A year where aid rose and the appropriation rose with it and a year where aid was flat and the town covered the difference are different facts about the world and identical facts on the page. — closes: the Town’s FY-end recap (Form A-1) beside the Cherry Sheet for the same year, which states estimated and actual receipts on one page.
money_inWhether a year's special education overrun on the general fund measures surprise, or how much was charged to the circuit breaker account at the closeMEASURED (/special-education/special-education-overruns): the need a Special Education Reserve Fund is sized against is the general fund's spending past its vote, line by line, after the circuit breaker account (fund 2640) and the grants paid their share. The circuit breaker account paid tuition in every year FY2023-FY2026, and in FY2026 it paid through a single year-end reclassification of collaborative tuition rather than through invoices during the year (/special-education/sped-all-funds). So how much of a year's tuition lands on the general fund, and therefore that year's overrun, turns partly on a charge decided at the close. Set the account's tuition back on the line and FY2024's need is $619,020 rather than $152,724. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the amount charged each year follows a rule (the reimbursement received, a planned share, whatever kept the general fund within its vote), so the year-to-year spread of the general fund need cannot be separated from the spread of that choice. — closes: the district's circuit breaker spending plan for each year, set before the year began, against which the year-end charge can be compared.
money_inWhether an unspent school grant budget was carried into the next grant year or simply never drawnMEASURED: the grants named for FY2023 and FY2024 spent less than the budget the ledger loaded for them (/school-all-funds/unspent-by-fund). A loaded budget is not always the award -- two FY2026 funds each carry a Title I budget and one has spent nothing -- and some federal grants allow a carryover into the next year's grant, so the shortfall is not established as money lost. — closes: DESE's grant award notices, final expenditure reports and carryover approvals for each school grant, FY2023-FY2026.
money_inWhether the district charges anything for music, and what an instrument costs a familyA resident told the School Committee on 26 February 2025 that "Instruments cost a lot, you need reeds and that can cost $50 a semester", and that band families "just aren’t paying anything directly to the school". That establishes music as a real household cost and establishes nothing about a district charge: no music fee, instrument rental rate or materials fee appears anywhere in this archive. A cost paid to a shop and a fee paid to the district are different things and neither is currently priced. — closes: the district’s music program fee schedule for 2026-27, or a statement that it charges no music fee and rents no instruments.
money_inWhether the school choice fund’s SCH. CHOICE BUS FEE account is where the student bus fees are bookedIn the school special funds year-end reports, fund 1308 (school choice) carries revenue account 437601, SCH. CHOICE BUS FEE. It took in nothing in FY2023 and FY2024, began receiving money in FY2025 -- the year the first student bus fees fell due -- and received again in FY2026, while the town general fund's STUDENTBUS revenue account shows nothing. That timing fits the fees and does not establish them: the account is named for school choice, and a fee charged only to school choice students would book the same way. Narrows 'Where bus fee receipts are booked' without closing it. — closes: the Town Accountant's definition of account 1308-437601, or the cash receipts detail behind it for FY2025 and FY2026 showing whether the deposits are the RevTrak and check payments for the student bus fee.
money_inWhich Lunenburg budget lines the circuit breaker reimbursement offsetsdese_circuit_breaker gives the reimbursement the district receives for high-cost special education placements, split into instruction and tuition against transportation, FY2006 to FY2026. It is real money and it is not in the general fund appropriation the town votes. Rule 11: a tuition line that fell because circuit breaker rose is not a line that got cheaper, and the budget document cannot tell the two apart. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED is which lines it lands against, or whether the district budgets net of it — the workbook nets other lines down against expected receipts and says so in its own comments column, so this is not a hypothetical. — closes: the district’s circuit breaker revolving fund cashbook for the year, which shows what the receipt was spent on.
money_inWhich competitive DESE grants Lunenburg applied for and did not winDESE's award documents name only the districts that won. Comparison districts won competitive grants in FY2026 and FY2027 that Lunenburg did not (/school-all-funds/grants-others-receive), and nothing published says whether the district applied for them. — closes: the district's list of the DESE grant applications it submitted, by year, with each outcome
money_inWhich competitive state and federal grants the school district applied for and won, by yearDESE's allocation pages list formula entitlements only, and its open-grants list shows what is open now, not who was awarded. So the grant comparison (/school-all-funds/grants-others-receive) cannot compare what Lunenburg applied for or won against other districts. — closes: the district's grants list by year, with the application and award notice for each competitive grant, and DESE's award listings for the same years.
money_inWhich departments’ unspent appropriations produced the free cashMoney appropriated and not spent is the largest single component of Lunenburg’s free cash — 47% of five years of it, and 66% of the record 2025 certification. It is published as one town-wide figure across 67 departments. Prudence, a post left vacant, a project that slipped into the next year and a line that was over-budgeted from the start are four different facts about the world and one number on the page. — closes: the period 13 general ledger, showing budget, expended and turnback for each department at the year-end close.
money_inWhich fund and account each field-rental receipt from Lunenburg Youth Soccer was posted to, and whether the $15,000 turf contribution is inside or beside themThe district’s records-request answer lists seven receipts, FY2024–FY2026, $39,073.50 in all, with one MUNIS reference; the town’s FY26 special-revenue report carries fund 1306 School Facilities Use Revolving and fund 1545 Artificial Turf Revolving as balances only — closes: the journal detail export for funds 1306 and 1545, FY2024–FY2026, the same report the archive holds for fund 1301
money_inWhich fund pays the teacher salaries a district charges to grants and revolving accounts?DESE’s function-code file splits spending into general fund and grants-plus-revolving, and the gap between comparable districts is large: Harvard charges $2,482 per pupil of TEACHER salaries to grants and revolving funds where Lunenburg charges $363 (FY2025, over total FTE pupils). That single line is the largest part, about half, of the difference in what the two draw from outside the appropriation. (Corrected 15 October 2026: this row said $4,964 and $726, each exactly double -- DESE's category subtotal row had been summed with its own line items.) The file does not say WHICH fund — a specific grant, school choice tuition received, a tuition agreement — and the answer decides whether it is something Lunenburg could pursue or a feature of one district’s circumstances. — closes: DESE’s End of Year Pupil and Financial Report for the district, which reports spending by individual fund.
money_inWhich of the FY2011 receipts the Town collected are TAXES & EXCISES, which are FEES, and which are NON RECURRING REVENUE?Page 58 of the FY2011 annual town report prints 90 receipt lines under ten block headings and then a nine-category SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS footed to a GRAND TOTAL of $27,388,537.87. The summary ties to the cent, and every detail figure on the page is now transcribed, but the page never says which detail line belongs to which category and the headings are not the categories — ten blocks against nine categories, one block unheaded, and FEES naming both a block and a category without the two agreeing. Five categories can be reproduced exactly (LICENSES AND PERMITS, STATE REVENUE, SPECIAL ASSESSMENTS, INVESTMENT INCOME, TRANSFER FROM OTHER FUNDS); four cannot. TAXES & EXCISES comes out $23,947.19 OVER its printed total, FINES & FORFEITS $2,025.00 SHORT, and FEES ($502,520.65) and NON RECURRING REVENUE ($71,325.29) cannot be reconstructed by any grouping the page states. So the town’s own revenue mix for FY2011 — how much is tax, how much is fee, how much is one-off — cannot be read off the document that reports it. This is the same limit already registered for FY2016, FY2020 and FY2021 and it recurs because the format does. — closes: the Treasurer’s or Accountant’s FY2011 receipts detail as the accounting system prints it, with each receipt account carrying its revenue classification (a MUNIS revenue report by account), which is the only document that states the mapping rather than assuming it.
money_inWhich of the FY2020 receipts the Town collected are TAXES & EXCISES, which are FEES, and which are NON RECURRING REVENUE?The Treasurer's FY2020 receipts page (annual town report PDF p24) prints 100 line items in three free-form label/amount columns with NO column header, and a SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS block of nine categories footing to a GRAND TOTAL of $43,089,202.54. Both halves of the page were read off its own embedded bitmap on 2 October 2026 and both close to the cent: the 100 detail lines add to the GRAND TOTAL, and so, separately, do the nine summary lines. Six of the nine categories are defined by a heading the page prints above their lines and each foots exactly -- licenses and permits $331,254.75 (19 lines), state revenue $9,790,141.52 (12), special assessments $68,681.50 (3), fines and forfeits $37,182.61 (4), investment income $102,340.41 (1) and transfers from other funds $2,291,492.46 (1). The other three print no heading that separates them, and their 60 lines foot as ONE block to $30,468,109.29, the sum of the three printed category totals. A residual does fit -- moving SUPPL TAX-NEW CONSTRUCTION $10,057.81 out of taxes and $100,180.88 of RESCUE WAGON out of non-recurring would close all three -- but that is arithmetic choosing a grouping rather than the document stating one, and other partitions fit the same three printed totals equally well. So we can say what the town took in, and not how it classified 60 of the lines. This is the SAME gap already registered for FY2021 and it is a property of the form, not of one year. -- closes: the Treasurer's own receipts workbook for FY2020, the file the page is printed from, which carries the category each line is coded to. Not published; a records request to the Town Treasurer would obtain it.
money_inWhich of the FY2021 receipts the Town collected are TAXES & EXCISES, which are FEES, and which are NON RECURRING REVENUE?The Treasurer's FY2021 receipts page (annual town report PDF p25) prints 100 line items in three free-form label/amount columns with NO column header, and a SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS block of nine categories footing to a GRAND TOTAL of $44,252,049.61. Six of the nine categories are defined by a heading the page prints above the lines and each foots exactly -- licenses and permits, state revenue, special assessments, fines and forfeits, investment income, transfers from other funds. The other three print no heading that separates them, and their 60 lines foot as one block to $31,988,239.19. A residual does fit -- the taxes/interest/demands lines plus prior year excise and prior year interest, LESS supplemental tax on new construction, is $31,200,742.70 to the cent -- but that is arithmetic choosing a grouping rather than the document stating one, and other partitions fit the same three printed totals equally well. So we can say what the town took in, and not how it classified 60 of the lines. -- closes: the Treasurer's own receipts workbook for FY2021, the file the page is printed from, which carries the category each line is coded to. Not published; a records request to the Town Treasurer would obtain it.
money_inWhich school special revenue funds the period-13 special funds report leaves outThe FY2023 annual town report's special revenue schedule prints $3,667,636 received and $4,333,280 spent across every school special revenue fund; the MUNIS period-13 special funds report for the same year, delivered 6 October 2026, carries $2,440,883 and $2,962,716. The difference is funds that report does not carry -- among them, the annual report's FY22 ESSER II #115, FY22 ARP Idea #252 and FY22 Idea ARP #264 rows have no fund of that name or number in the MUNIS report. And the FY2026 report books $59,333 of grant revenue against $557,427 of grant spending. A reimbursement booked after the close, a grant receipt held in a fund outside the report, and both together all fit; the report cannot separate them, so whether the schools spend the grant money that comes in can be said only for the funds it carries. Measured in /analysis/spending-what-comes-in. — closes: the MUNIS period-13 revenue and expense report for EVERY school special revenue fund, FY2023 to FY2026, with each fund's opening and closing balance (or the trial balance for funds 2xxx at each close).
money_inWhy Chapter 70 aid moved by more than the components DESE publishes, in FY2010, FY2011, FY2012 and FY2019DESE’s Chapter 70 trends workbook prints the aid build-up as named increments — foundation aid, down payment aid, growth aid, target aid phase-in, minimum aid — and in fifteen of the nineteen differenced years they sum to the change in aid to the dollar. In four they do not. FY2010 and FY2011 carry a separate c70aidreduct column of −$92,416 and −$279,101, and only the first of the two accounts for its year; FY2012 moved +$24,149 with every increment printed as zero; FY2019 moved $13,365 more than its single increment. The workbook prints no residual line, so the difference has no name in the source. It matters because this page reads the components to say what the formula did, and in those four years the components do not add up to what it did. — closes: DESE’s Chapter 70 aid calculation worksheet for FY2010, FY2011, FY2012 and FY2019, which states every adjustment applied to a district between the prior year’s aid and the current year’s.
money_inWhy DLS certifies a different amount from the free cash its own proof identifiesThe Division of Local Services’ free cash proof cross-foots exactly: in all 45 town-years of the nine-town set the eleven component lines sum, to the cent, to the workbook’s own Identified Free Cash July 1,. But that is not the figure DLS certifies. Current Year Calculation — the number the Town quotes, the number the Finance Director announced, and the number that carries into the next year — differs from it in all 45, by $361,912 for Lunenburg in 2025 and by 69% for Uxbridge in 2024. The workbook prints no reconciling line, and nothing in this archive states what the adjustment is. — closes: DLS’s free cash certification letter to the Town, which states the adjustments made between the balance sheet the Town submitted and the amount certified.
money_inWhy Lunenburg's IDEA special education allocation per pupil is lower than most comparable districts'MEASURED (/school-all-funds/grant-allocations-compared): DESE's IDEA allocation divided by DESE's October headcount puts Lunenburg below the median of its comparison districts in every year that can be compared since FY2017. NOT ESTABLISHED: why. DESE's eligibility text names enrolment in public and private schools and children in poverty as inputs; our divisor counts only pupils enrolled in the district, and the formula's other parts are not on DESE's allocation pages. A smaller resident count, a smaller poverty count or a historical base amount all fit. — closes: DESE's IDEA Part B allocation calculation for Lunenburg, FY2017-FY2027, showing each input.
money_inWhy did the circuit breaker and the special education grants pay a smaller share of special education in FY2026 than in FY2023?The school journal shows the share of special education postings outside the general fund falling over FY2023-FY2026 (/special-education/sped-all-funds), and that in FY2026 the circuit breaker fund paid through a single year-end reclassification of collaborative tuition rather than through invoices during the year. A smaller reimbursement, a balance held back for the next year, and costs moved to other accounts all fit the same postings, and nothing in a ledger says which. — closes: the district’s circuit breaker and IDEA spending plans for FY2023-FY2026, and the circuit breaker account statement for each year.
money_inWhy did the federal special education grant pay a private placement in FY2026 that the general fund paid in FY2025, and did the FY2026 budget expect it?MEASURED in the school journal: May Institute was paid $333,614 in FY2025 ($318,255 from the general fund, $15,359 from the circuit breaker) and $345,856 in FY2026 -- $287,108 of it from the FY2026 IDEA grant (fund 2814, on a contracted services account) and $58,748 from the general fund. No IDEA grant fund paid any placement in FY2023-FY2025. The FY2026 private tuition line was voted at $988,630 and left $522,629, the largest leftover on any school account, and the grant payment is more than half of it. A payee is not a child: the journal cannot say how many students May Institute served or whether the service changed. On 16 September 2026 a speaker at the School Committee said the unexpended funds looked to be "in our private school tuitions" and spoke of "taking certain tuitions out of the grants" (machine captions, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XY8Ru12S9Xg&t=729s). Not established: whether the budget assumed the grant would pay (the budget book plans no grant offset on private tuition) or the switch was made during the year. — closes: the district's FY2026 IDEA (fund code 240) grant application and its DESE-approved budget, which name what the grant was planned to pay for.
money_inWhy does DESE's FY2024 figure for out-of-district tuition paid from funds other than the general fund exceed what the circuit breaker account paid by exactly the FY2024 circuit breaker payment?DESE's End of Year Financial Report reports FY2024 tuition (functions 9300 and 9400) paid from funds other than the general fund. The town's year-end report for the school special funds shows what the circuit breaker account (fund 2640) paid in tuition that year. The remainder between the two is, to the dollar, the circuit breaker payment DESE's reimbursement file lists for FY2024; in FY2023 and FY2025 the remainder is small. The figures are computed, not typed, in the report's payload under circuit_breaker.unexplained. It may be a coincidence, a second fund, or the receipt reported as an expenditure; nothing in this archive distinguishes them, so /analysis/special-education-costs shows the figure as 'other funds' and says it cannot explain it. Computed in scripts/build_sped_costs.py, which refuses to print the sentence if the equality stops holding. — closes: the district's FY2024 End of Year Financial Report as submitted to DESE (Schedule 1 by fund), or the school special funds year-end report for any fund other than 2640 that paid tuition in FY2024.
money_inWhy local receipts come in above the town’s own estimateThe state's free cash proof shows receipts above the town's estimate (its line CL#6) as one of the largest components of Lunenburg's free cash in every one of the five years it covers, and above a million dollars in four of them. On 28 May 2026 a Finance Committee member told the committee the town had not collected less than four million dollars in local receipts in ten years, against a current estimate of 3.535 million. Three readings fit the same line: an estimate set low on purpose as a buffer; receipts that grew faster than any forecast could know; or one-time receipts that should not be estimated at all. They imply different things about how much of each year's free cash is predictable, and so about how much the budget could count on. Measured in /analysis/sitting-on-money. — closes: the town's local receipts estimate against actual collections, by category, for each year -- the local receipts page of each year's Tax Rate Recapitulation beside DLS Schedule A.
money_inWhy the Town’s undesignated fund balance and DLS’s free cash differTwo publishers describe the same 30 June balance sheet and print three different figures. The Town’s annual report roll-forward gives an undesignated fund balance of $4,236,488.24 at 30 June 2025; DLS identifies $3,716,282 of free cash on the same date and certifies $3,354,370. Each worksheet cross-foots exactly to its own printed total, and the FY2024 report’s closing balance is the FY2025 report’s opening one to the cent — so neither is in error, and no document in this archive prints a line between any pair of the three. — closes: the Town’s free cash submission to DLS (the balance sheet and the reconciliation of receivables and deferred revenue that accompanies it).
money_inWhy the district's grant history and DESE's allocations disagree for Lunenburg's special education grantsMEASURED: the district's own grants history (sources/data/grants-history.csv, read from the superintendent's FY25 budget update, pp. 32-36, and the FY24 presentation, p. 16) and DESE's entitlement allocation pages (sources/data/dese-entitlement-allocations.csv, every year reconciled to DESE's by-district page) disagree for Lunenburg. IDEA 240: FY2020 $367,980 in the budget book against $369,440 at DESE; FY2024 $418,237 against $420,163; FY2021-FY2023 agree. Early childhood 262: FY2020 $12,281 vs $12,303, FY2021 $12,368 vs $12,401, FY2023 $13,133 vs $13,083, FY2024 $13,245 vs $13,325; FY2022 agrees at $12,500. ARP IDEA: the budget book lists $88,330 and $8,229 in each of FY2020, FY2021 and FY2022, and $87,888 on grant 252 in FY2023; DESE prints 252 ($88,330) and 264 ($8,229) for FY2022 only. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: why. An allocation DESE revised after the book was printed, the book reporting a different stage (a budgeted or amended award, a carryover, a draw) under the same name, or a multi-year grant printed in each year it was spent all fit; nothing here tests any of them, and no earlier version of these pages is held here -- our weekly snapshots begin 23 October 2026. FY2018 IDEA cannot be checked across views: DESE's by-fund-code page for 0240 FY2018 answers with its server error page. -- closes: the grant award letters (DESE's GEM$ project award and any amendments) for funds 240, 262, 252 and 264, FY2020-FY2024, which state the amount awarded and its period.
money_inWhy the general fund’s starting budget grew more slowly than the levy limit, FY2010 to FY2025Measured from the general fund history against the Division of Local Services’ certified levy limits, the whole starting budget grew more slowly each year, on average, than the levy limit did — even with the FY2025 override taken back out of the limit. Three readings fit: the rest of the revenue (state aid, local receipts, free cash) grew more slowly than the levy; the town levied below its limit; or money raised under the limit went outside the general fund operating budget, to capital articles or enterprise subsidies. They imply different things about how much room the levy has left. Measured in /analysis/department-budgets. — closes: the Tax Rate Recapitulation for each fiscal year, which states the levy actually raised, the excess levy capacity and every other source the budget was balanced with.
money_inWould regionalising change what the state sends Lunenburg, and by how much?This is among the most common arguments made about the deficit and the archive cannot price the whole of it. Regional districts receive regional transportation reimbursement under c.71 s16C that single-town districts do not, and that part IS held: the DLS Cherry Sheet line, FY2010-FY2027, priced in the row 'What would regionalising actually be worth to Lunenburg...'. What is not held is how the Chapter 70 formula would treat a newly regionalised district, or the busing cost a regional district takes on against the reimbursement. Per-pupil SPENDING is held and is a different quantity: it says what a district spends, not what the state sends. — closes: DESE guidance on how the Chapter 70 formula treats a newly regionalised district, and a regional district's own budget stating transportation cost beside the reimbursement.

money_outHow fast did the price of out-of-district tuition and of school bus contracts rise, year by year?/school-spending-history/inflation-and-school-costs measures each kind of school spending, FY2009 to FY2025, against a published price index for that kind of thing -- school pay, public employers’ benefits, groceries, home energy -- and has none for tuition or buses. The state’s Operational Services Division sets approved special education school prices by an inflation factor each year but publishes only the current year’s estimate (mass.gov answered 404 for every earlier year asked, 20 October 2026), and the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes no price index for school bus transportation. Both are measured against household prices instead, which are not what a school pays. Every index used is national or regional, not Lunenburg’s own price, and none says how much of any rise was price rather than more placements, more buses or more staff. — closes: the Operational Services Division’s approved price for each placement Lunenburg paid, by fiscal year, and each year’s bus contract with its daily rate per bus and the number of buses, from the Business Office.
money_outHow is the FY2027 half-time athletic director paid, and is any of it offset from the athletic fee fund as FY2026 was?MEASURED: for FY2026 the director line was voted $74,406, $20,407 below its level-service $94,813, and meetings described it as the director's salary less a $20,000 offset from the athletic revolving fund (School Committee video, 16 April 2025; Finance Committee video, 20 March 2025); the journal shows no fee-fund payment to the director that year. For FY2027 the drafts held propose between $20,000 and $98,131 for the line, the last (25 March 2026) $20,000, and a half-time director was appointed from 1 August 2026. Shown on /athletics/athletic-director. — closes: the FY2027 school budget as voted, and the half-time director's appointment terms.
money_outHow many athletic bus trips each sport took, and what each trip costThe district's sport-by-sport workbook gives transportation dollars per sport for FY2024 to FY2026 as sums of charges, and the posted schedules (ArbiterLive) list each team's away games and venues from FY2022. /analysis/transportation prices the schedules at the Dee Bus contract's per-mile and per-hour rates as our estimate, with the waiting hours an assumption from the bid form. What no document shows is which games actually got a bus, whether teams shared one, how long each bus waited, and what each charge on the sheet was. — closes: the Dee Bus athletic and field-trip invoices for FY2024 to FY2026, with date, team, miles and waiting hours per trip, from the Business Office
money_outHow many vans, monitors and routes special education transportation pays for, and at what ratesThe general fund special education transportation line is the only published figure: voted and spent, by year. money_outHow much of DESE’s general fund figure for Lunenburg the school budget paid, and how much other town budgets paidDESE’s per-pupil figure counts general fund spending on the schools whoever paid it: insurance for retired school staff (function 5250) is in it, and in FY2026 the town carries that insurance in its own insurance department (SCHRETHLTH), not in the school appropriation. DESE’s expenditures-by-function file has one GEN_FUND column and does not say which budget paid which line, so the school appropriation divided by pupils is not DESE’s figure a pupil, and the difference cannot be itemised from it. Found building /school-spending/per-pupil-line-by-line. — closes: the district’s End of Year Financial Report as filed with DESE, whose Schedule 1 reports expenditures by the school committee and, separately, expenditures by city or town (part B, row 1016 of DESE’s FY2025 form), for the same year.
money_outHow much of Harvard’s higher spending a pupil comes from being a smaller districtHarvard spends more a pupil than Lunenburg on DESE’s all-funds measure, and divides its spending among fewer pupils. A smaller district spreads costs that do not shrink with enrolment — a principal, a building, a superintendent’s office — over fewer pupils, so part of any per-pupil gap may be scale rather than programme, and DESE’s function-code file cannot say how much: it reports dollars by function, not which costs are fixed. The Bromfield shelf states this as a hypothesis and tests nothing. — closes: nothing published settles it; DESE’s staffing by job classification and salary (EPIMS) for both districts, school by school, would bound the share that is fixed posts.

money_outHow much of Lunenburg's debt at the end of 1989 sat inside the debt limit, and how much outside it?The inside/outside-the-limit split of 2001-2010 is not in the 1989 report. Its debt pages (p39-p40) mark only INTEREST (EXEMPTED) on the two elementary school remodelling issues and the ambulance (p40); the text was searched for debt limit, inside and exempt and returned nothing else (sources/data/report-tables/1989/). — closes: the Treasurer's debt statement for 1989, or the Town's Schedule A filed with the Department of Revenue.
money_outHow much of a receiving district’s per-pupil spending Lunenburg actually pays177 Lunenburg children were educated outside Lunenburg Public Schools in FY2026 and DESE publishes what each receiving district spends for every pupil, all funds. It does not publish what LUNENBURG pays towards any of it, and the two are different quantities by construction: a receiving district’s per-pupil figure is its whole spending over its whole pupil count, paid for by its own levy, its own Chapter 70 aid, its grants and its revolving funds as well as by any tuition or assessment. Lunenburg’s side arrives as three unlike mechanisms — a member-town assessment for Montachusett, a school choice tuition set by statute, and a charter tuition set by formula — and none of them equals the receiving district’s per-pupil figure. So the honest statement is that the districts our children go to spend more for each pupil than Lunenburg does; what a Lunenburg child costs the town at each of them cannot be read off it. — closes: the Town’s cherry sheet assessment detail for the fiscal year, which states the charter tuition, school choice tuition and regional assessment by receiving district, set beside DESE’s End of Year Financial Report for each of those districts.
money_outHow much of a school budget stops being spent when a student leavesA student leaving removes revenue at once and in full. It removes cost only where a staffing or programme decision is taken, and nothing published says at what enrollment a class section is removed, a bus route is dropped or a teacher is not replaced. So the avoidable share of a per-pupil figure is an assumption in every scenario on this site, and it is the input the answer is most sensitive to: at the FY2027 appropriation per pupil, the difference between assuming none of it is avoidable and assuming all of it is is larger than the entire revenue effect being modelled. — closes: the district’s own staffing and section plan by grade — the document behind the School Committee’s 16 April 2025 discussion of "each grade, their size, and potential seats" — which states the class sizes at which a section is added or removed.
money_outHow much of each earlier year’s ski team cost was Lunenburg’s, and how much the other co-op towns’?The district’s by-sport workbook prints one figure for the ski team and it is the whole four-town co-op’s cost — $12,984 in FY2025, $10,960 in FY2024. The only invoice held is the 2025-26 one, where Lunenburg’s share was 21.4%. Nothing says any earlier year split the same way, or that the co-op had the same members — closes: the co-op invoices for the earlier seasons, which the athletic department issues and holds
money_outHow much of the $236,766.94 still encumbered in the FY2026 school general fund at period 13 will be paid, how much released to the surplus, and how much carried into FY2027?The FY2026 period-13 MUNIS report for department 300 (sources/data/munis-school-ytd.csv), run on 6 October 2026, shows $482,118.07 unspent and $236,766.94 still encumbered across 27 accounts -- the largest electricity ($62,362.13) and collaborative tuitions ($58,708.07). Between the period-12 run of 1 September 2026 and that run, spending did not move in any account and one encumbrance of $16.95 was released, so the FY26 school surplus is still anywhere from $482,118.07 to $718,885.01. The FY2025 report run the same day shows nothing encumbered. A ledger shows a commitment, not whether it will be paid, cancelled or carried forward, and which of those happens decides the surplus. /analysis/fy26-school-surplus. — closes: the FY2026 period-13 report for department 300 run again after the year-end close, and the Town Accountant's list of FY2026 encumbrances carried forward into FY2027, by account.
money_outHow much of the rise in school costs was higher prices, and how much was more of what the schools buy?/school-spending-history/inflation-and-school-costs sets each kind of school spending, FY2009 to FY2025, against Boston-area household prices, and compares the largest recurring bills in the school MUNIS journal payment for payment, FY2023 to FY2026. Both measure dollars, not prices. A budget line is price times quantity; a matched bill holds the payee, the account and the number of payments a year constant, but not what each payment buys -- the buses run each day (the Dee Bus row), the subscribers on each health plan tier (the enrollment row), the kilowatt-hours. And household prices are not what a school pays for salaries, insurance or tuition (the constant-dollars row). So the page can say which costs grew faster than prices; it cannot say how much of any rise was price, and so cannot say how much of the school deficit -- the level-service budget less the appropriation -- rising prices produced. — closes: the district’s level-service budget worksheets for each year, with every line’s price and quantity assumptions, and the rate sheets behind each recurring bill (daily rate per bus and buses run, premium per tier and subscribers, rate per kWh), from the Business Office.
money_outHow much was in the school circuit breaker fund on 30 June 2025 and 30 June 2026, and how much of it would have expired unspent?The school journal shows the fund's receipts and payments from FY2023 -- FY2025 took in the most, and FY2026 paid almost nothing from it until $333,494.89 of tuition was charged to it on 29 June 2026 -- but not its opening balance, so what would have lapsed under the one-year carry-forward the district described to the Finance Committee on 22 October 2026 cannot be computed. -- closes: the Town Accountant's fund 2640 balance at each year end, FY2022 to FY2026, with receipts by service year.
money_outHow the Monty Tech assessment splits between operating, transportation and capitalA regional assessment is four parts, and the district names them: required minimum contribution set by the state, transportation and other operating above minimum net school spending, capital outlay, and bonds. The split is published for FY2024, FY2026 and FY2027 in the district’s own budget books, and for FY2023 it was itemised in prose at a Finance Committee meeting. Every other year holds only the total. That includes FY2025, and it includes all eleven annual-report years FY2011 to FY2022 — so for the whole of the series this project charts, the roughly 4-10% of the assessment sitting above the state minimum cannot be attributed to transportation, to capital or to debt. It matters because those three behave nothing alike: one tracks a busing contract, one is voted year by year, and one is fixed until it ends. — closes: the district’s annual assessment certification to each member town, which states the four components separately; the Town Accountant receives one every year and the district retains all of them.
money_outHow the district built its FY2027 athletic transportation estimateOn 26 August 2026 the Superintendent put restoring high school athletic buses at about $58,880, attributing the lower figure to scheduling competitions closer to Lunenburg, more home competitions, and estimating from actual schedules and prior-year spring costs. /analysis/transportation tests the first two reasons against the posted schedules and prices the schedules with the contract's rates, but most of its result is the hours a bus waits, which is an assumption. Without the worksheet behind the estimate, the two cannot be set side by side assumption for assumption. — closes: the worksheet or calculation behind the $58,880 FY2027 athletic transportation estimate (trips, miles and waiting hours by team), from the Superintendent's office.
money_outHow the district’s own accounts add up to the net school spending DESE reportsNARROWED 5 October 2026 for FY2024. the Finance Committee files received by records request on 4 October 2026 (sources/budget-workbooks/finance-committee/, see its PROVENANCE note) include the district's FY24 End of Year Financial Report workbook, whose own Schedule 19 states net school spending as 22,496,198 (reports sheet, row 28) -- a working copy, so DESE's filed figure governs. Net school spending excludes debt service, capital, transportation and food service — stated in the town’s own record, to the Finance Committee on 20 March 2024: “This is the minimum spending every school district must spend not including debt services, capital transportation, meals.” Because of those exclusions no figure in the town’s appropriation, the district’s budget book or the MUNIS ledger equals the net school spending DESE reports, and nothing in this archive maps the district’s line items onto DESE’s definition. So a reader cannot get from a budget line they can see to the one number the state enforces. — closes: the district’s End of Year Financial Report as filed with DESE, whose schedules derive net school spending from the district’s own accounts line by line; requestable from the Superintendent’s office or from DESE.
money_outSchool share of Medicare, active health insurance and the insurance reservesFive of the seven FY2026 insurance accounts — active health insurance, Medicare, life insurance, insurance cost control and Public Employee Committee expenses — carry nothing in their names that says which side of the town they are for, so the school portion of them is not separable in any year. — closes: The town’s Chapter 32B enrollment schedule, which counts insured employees and retirees by department.
money_outSchool share of the pensioninside WRRS · town and school staff together, no published split
money_outSchool share of the town’s health insurance before FY2026The town’s insurance department prints one undivided Health Insurance CH 32B line in fifteen of the sixteen annual reports · a school share is named only in the FY2023 report and in the FY2026 ledger, so no year between them can be split. — closes: The town’s Chapter 32B enrollment schedule, which counts insured employees and retirees by department and would split every year rather than the two that happened to be printed.
money_outWas the 18-month budget spent on pace: what did the town spend in the six months January-June 1974 against what was left?The accountant's schedule (p57-60) prints the 18-month funds available, the amount expended through December 31, 1973 (twelve of the eighteen months) and the balance at January 1, 1974. The report goes to press before June 30, 1974, so the second period's spending is not in any edition's table; the 1974 edition may print the 18-month close. Searched the whole text for 18 month and eighteen: p56-60, p66, p121 (sources/data/report-tables/1973/). — closes: the 1974 annual town report's statement of the 18-month fiscal year ended June 30, 1974.
money_outWas the FY2026 school surplus thrift — did discretionary spending slow late in the year?A speaker at the School Committee on 7 October 2026 said, per our machine captions, "We were thrifty"; no posted minutes record a decision to hold FY2026 spending. The period-13 ledger shows where money was left (by our category table, 59% of it in supplies, upkeep and equipment) but only as year-end totals, so restraint, a postponed project and a line budgeted high look identical. The school journal by month is now held, and it shows WHEN: spending fell behind its usual pace from February (40.2% of the budget left at the end of March against about 33% in FY2023 and FY2024), and ten building payees used every year were paid under half as usual. It cannot show whether anyone DECIDED to hold spending. — closes: any written or minuted instruction in FY2026 to hold, defer or freeze school purchasing, with its date.
money_outWere the building jobs the schools usually pay for, and the purchase orders closed unpaid, done another way in FY2026 — or not done?The journal shows ten payees used every year paid under half as usual in FY2026, five of them nothing (security service, door systems, boiler inspections, piano tuning, irrigation), and $67,393 of purchase orders on contracted building services released unpaid, $37,626 of them carried in from FY2025. A payment from another account, a new vendor record, a warranty or a dropped job all look the same in a ledger. Asked by the Finance Committee for each contract and its end date, the district named five contractors and gave no dates — closes: the facilities work orders for FY2026, by building and job, and each service contract with its scope and term
money_outWhat DESE’s per-pupil figure buysDESE publishes dollars over a pupil count, by function, for every district. It does not publish what those dollars bought: a Teachers line is not a class size, an Instructional Materials line is not a textbook count, and a Paraprofessional FTE is not a person or a caseload. So Lunenburg spending $226 a pupil on instructional materials, equipment and technology against a statewide median of $626 is a measured difference in money and not a measured difference in what children have. Rule 7’s standing form: dollars are not services. — closes: the district’s own inventory and purchasing records for the materials and technology line, which would say what was bought and when.
money_outWhat Lunenburg pays in school choice sending tuition, and for how many childrenThe town pays tuition to every district a Lunenburg child chooses into, and that money is assessed rather than appropriated: it sits inside the single State Assessments (Outside Operating FY27) line of $1,069,349 in the FY2027 Town Meeting booklet, which is never broken out. The archive now holds DESE’s count of the children — 58 leaving under school choice in SY2026 — and still not one figure for what they cost. The statutory base rate is $5,000 a child under M.G.L. c.76 §12B and is higher for special education, and no document in this archive states either, so every scenario of students transferring out is priced on an assumption. — closes: DLS Cherry Sheet CS 1-EB (estimated charges) for Lunenburg, which prints the school choice sending assessment on its own line.
money_outWhat Lunenburg’s Chapter 32B §19 Public Employee Committee agreement actually sets — the premium split, the opt-out payment, and the plan menuCLOSED 6 October 2026 for FY27–FY29. The memorandum of agreement (sources/contracts/pdf/pec-agreement-fy27-fy29.pdf, 5 October) sets the plan menu, in-network cost-sharing, the HSA contribution, the $96 Medicare Part B reimbursement and the splits — 75/25 for active plans and Managed Blue for Seniors, 50/50 for Medex — 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2029. Its two blank attachments arrived on 6 October from the Town’s Human Resources Director, who wrote that ""The Benefit Summaries are Attachment A, and the Opt-Out Policy is Attachment B"": four Blue Cross summaries of benefits for the four active plans (pec-fy27-attachment-a-1 to -4) and the FY27 opt-out guidelines (pec-fy27-attachment-b-opt-out-policy.pdf), which pay $3,000 for individual coverage, $6,000 for family and $3,000 for a change from family to individual. Still open: summaries for the two Medicare plans, registered separately. — closes: closed by the documents named.
money_outWhat Lunenburg’s net school spending actually was in the two most recent yearsDESE publishes net school spending against the Chapter 70 requirement for thirty-three fiscal years, and the last two of them are BUDGETED rather than actual — the column carries a stage flag saying so. So the most recent MEASURED position Lunenburg has against the state is FY2024, and every statement about where the town sits NOW rests on a budget somebody voted rather than on money anybody spent. The two may not be differenced and are never drawn as one line, which is why /what-the-state-requires-us-to-spend carries them as separate series. — closes: DESE’s Chapter 70 district profile workbook for the year in which FY2025 moves into the actual column, published annually at educationtocareer.data.mass.gov; the district’s own End of Year Financial Report to DESE for FY2025 is the filing that produces it.
money_outWhat Monty Tech spends, and on whatLunenburg is assessed $1,334,521 for Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical in FY2026 and that figure is what the town is BILLED, not what educating 101 foundation pupils costs. PART OF THIS ROW HAS CLOSED. DESE’s RADAR district comparison publishes an all-funds per-pupil total for LEA 08320000 for FY2009 to FY2025 — seventeen consecutive years, every one of them summing to the workbook’s own printed in-district total — so the district’s per-pupil spending CAN now be tracked over time and set beside Lunenburg Public Schools’ own, measured the same way, which is what /what-other-districts-spend does. WHAT REMAINS OPEN is the composition and the attribution. RADAR gives ten per-pupil function columns and no dollars, no fund split and nothing specific to Lunenburg’s children; the archive holds two of the district’s own budget books — the FY2024 hearing book and the FY2027 presentation — so a FY24-to-FY27 view by DESE function code exists in dollars, with no year before FY2024 and nothing for the years between the two books. So what the district spends on a Lunenburg child, as against on any child, is still not established. — closes: Monty Tech’s annual budget book for each year, presented to its own School Committee and to the Lunenburg Finance Committee every March, and DESE’s End of Year Financial Report for LEA 08320000, which gives all-funds spending by function in dollars after the year closes.
money_outWhat a fee-funded school programme costs that is not booked to its own fundA revolving fund that takes in more than it spends covers the costs BOOKED TO IT, and nothing more (rule 11). The ledger can test whether the general fund also carries a programme's costs only where both book to the same programme-specific DESE function code, and among the schools' fee and lunch funds that is true of athletics alone (function 3510, where the general fund booked most of the four years' athletics spending). Extended day, after-school activities, facilities rental and adult education book their spending to function codes that name no programme -- 2000, 4000, 5200 -- so whether the general fund pays any of their custodians, utilities, administration or benefits cannot be shown either way. 'Pays its own way' therefore cannot be stated for any of them beyond their own books. Measured in /analysis/spending-what-comes-in. — closes: the district's indirect-cost allocation for each revolving programme, or a cost study listing the general fund accounts that carry part of each programme's cost.
money_outWhat a level-service budget for each town department would have cost, year by yearThe general fund history the Finance Committee supplied holds each department’s original budget, transfers, revised budget and actual spending, FY2010–FY2025, and no request: nothing in it says what a department asked for or what keeping its service level would have cost. The schools present a level-service budget, and its difference from the appropriation is what is reported as the school deficit. For the town’s departments no equivalent figure is in this archive for any year before FY2027 — the year the Town Manager asked department heads for level-service budgets (Finance Committee minutes, 12 February 2026) and the override questions covered town and school alike — so whether they would have shown a gap in earlier years cannot be measured, and the difference between the two sides may be one of process rather than of cost. — closes: each town department’s budget request as submitted to the Town Manager, with the Town Manager’s recommendation beside it, for each fiscal year, held by the Town Manager’s office.
money_outWhat any individual sport actually costsThree documents state per-sport costs and they disagree — see “Which of the three published per-sport athletics cost figures is correct”, which supersedes this row's original claim that the district's own athletics workbook was the only place per-sport costs appear. The district has publicly declined to stand behind the figures: School Committee minutes of 24 June 2026 record that community members 'have asked straightforward questions regarding the actual cost of middle school athletics' and that 'the answers have been inconsistent'. The one independent record we hold does not reconcile to the workbook — in FY2024 the revolving fund paid out $317,004 and the general fund carried $285,281 against a stated workbook cost of $351,643, and nothing published explains the difference. And the fund's own disbursements cannot close it either: each carries a warrant number and nothing else, with no vendor, no description, and not one mention of any sport across three years of transactions. So participations, fees, and the fund's total in and out are established; what a sport costs is not. — closes: the accounts-payable detail behind the athletics warrants — vendor and description per payment — which the town's accounting system holds and does not publish.
money_outWhat any special revenue fund boughtno expense report exists for these funds · purpose is presumed, never observed
money_outWhat did FLLAC’s (Keystone’s) payments buy, for how many Lunenburg students, at what rates?The FLLAC Educational Collaborative runs the Keystone program (the journal’s invoice numbers on this vendor carry KEY and its descriptions read TUITION FOR KEYSTONE). It was the largest special education payee in the school journal, FY2023-FY2026, paid from tuition and contracted related-services accounts, and its payments rose far faster than special education vendor payments overall (/special-education/sped-providers). WHAT THE DOCUMENTS SAY: the Finance Committee minutes of 14 March 2024 record a discussion of Keystone’s rates being raised almost 11%, and of how a 14% increase was absorbed the year before. Keystone’s quarterly updates to the School Committee (district-budget/docs/sc-meetings/, 2023-2025) report its census for ALL member districts together, and say it grew 11% from 2021 to September 2024. A 1 June 2023 memo to Keystone’s executive board, in the School Committee packet, records the collaborative buying 143 Joslin Street, Leominster, with a $5.377 million loan, for “the collaborative’s growing need for space”; Lunenburg’s superintendent voted for it as a board member. The collaborative agreement says tuition rates are set by Keystone’s board through its budget and sent to members by 30 June. WHAT IS NOT SETTLED: none of these gives Lunenburg’s own count of students at Keystone or its own tuition, and the stated rate and census changes are far smaller than the rise in Lunenburg’s payments. Whether the rest is more Lunenburg students, more services or longer placements is not in anything held. — closes: Keystone’s count of Lunenburg students and services by year, FY2023-FY2026, with its tuition rate sheets for each year.
money_outWhat did Lunenburg owe each year after June 1994, and how much of its debt sat inside the debt limit?report-debt holds a debt repayment schedule by issue and fiscal year from the 2001-2010 reports, and outstanding-debt the debt-limit split from FY2011 onward. The 1994 annual town report prints its bonded indebtedness issue by issue with fiscal 1995 payments only (p65) and the bonds authorized and unissued (p65); its text was searched on all 70 pages for repayment, schedule of, debt limit, outstanding and indebtedness and returned only p65 and the index entry (p3) (sources/data/report-tables/1994/). — closes: the Town's FY1994 Statement of Indebtedness as filed with the Division of Local Services.
money_outWhat did Lunenburg owe, by borrowing and by fiscal year, from FY2020 to FY2035?FY2019 PDF pages 49-52 print the whole forward debt repayment schedule -- about seventeen named borrowings against sixteen fiscal-year columns, each printed as PRINCIPAL / INTEREST / ADMIN FEE under a TOTAL row, on the order of 800 cells. It is fully self-proving (PRINCIPAL + INTEREST + ADMIN FEE = TOTAL, per issue per year, roughly 270 independent assertions). None of it has been read: debt-repayment-detail-refused.csv records 3 issue rows on p50 and 5 on p52 and no closing block, because the column header band at the top of each page sits inside the top 22.7% that the clipped render discarded. So the town's own forward debt service for sixteen years is published and unread. - closes: nothing from the Town is needed. The pages are legible at 150 dpi; this closes by reading them, after the document is re-OCR'd with the current renderer so the header band is visible. RESOLVED 2 October 2026: read in full, and the sizing in this row was wrong in every figure — it is FIFTEEN borrowings not seventeen, TWENTY-EIGHT fiscal years plus a TOTAL column not sixteen, 879 printed figures not ~800, and 213 issue-year identities not ~270. Measured off the pages. 198 of 213 close exactly and the 15 that miss by $1 are every one of them a Mass Water Pool trust line, which is displayed-dollar rounding and not a misread: bond principal, the column with no cents beneath it, ties exactly for 13 of 15 issues and the fifteen printed issue principals sum to $46,568,549 at ZERO tolerance.
money_outWhat did Lunenburg's capital project funds hold and spend in fiscal 1994?report-capital-projects reads the Capital Project Fund statement from the 2001-2010 reports. The 1994 annual town report prints none, and its combined balance sheet has no capital projects column (p31: GENERAL, SPECIAL REVENUE, TRUST and AGENCY, GENERAL LONG-TERM DEBT); article-funded projects appear instead as lines of the general fund appropriations schedule (e.g. p35 Landfill Closure 2/92 STM). Whether the town kept a separate capital projects fund in FY1994 is not established. Searched for capital project on all 70 pages: no hit (sources/data/report-tables/1994/). — closes: the Town's FY1994 audited financial statements (the independent audit, p33 Annual Audit) or its FY1994 Schedule A filed with the Division of Local Services.
money_outWhat did each Lunenburg town (non-school) employee earn in the period the 1997 report covers?report-gross-wages holds per-employee earnings. The 1997 annual town report's TOWN EMPLOYEES / REPORT OF WAGES PAID list is incomplete in our copy: PDF page 97 runs from AHO to GENDRON (read ENDRON) with the bottom of the page clipped, pages 98-99 are blank scans, no town total is printed, and the report's own index (p3: Wages 86-92) ends at folio 92, which is the last page of the SCHOOL list (PDF p96 prints 92). 52 town employees are read; the rest are not in the document we hold, and the list prints no year (sources/data/report-tables/1997/). — closes: a complete copy of the 1997 Annual Town Report (Town Clerk), or the Town's 1997 payroll register by employee.
money_outWhat did each Lunenburg town employee earn in 1959?report-gross-wages holds per-employee earnings from the 1995-2010 reports and FY2011-FY2025. The 1959 annual town report prints no wage list: the whole text (116 pages) was searched for wage, salary, payroll and gross and found only aggregates (the Treasurer's payments by department, p22-25; the accountant's wage lines, p26-36; the voted salaries, p58-59) and the School Personnel list (p103-106), which names staff, education and years of experience and prints no pay (sources/data/report-tables/1959/). — closes: the Town's calendar-1959 payroll register (totals by employee) from the Treasurer's office.
money_outWhat did each Lunenburg town employee earn in 1960?report-gross-wages holds per-employee earnings from the 1995-2010 reports and FY2011-FY2025. The 1960 annual town report (120 pages) prints no wage list: the whole text was searched for wages, payroll, gross, salary and employ and found only the Wages object lines inside the accountant's schedule (p26-36, by department, not by person), prose about payroll deductions (p74, p118) and the individual salaries of elected officers as voted lines (p58-59 budget; Selectmen's, Assessors', Treasurer's, Tax Collector's and Town Clerk's salaries) — closes: a payroll register or the Treasurer's warrants for calendar 1960
money_outWhat did each Lunenburg town employee earn in 1961?report-gross-wages holds per-employee earnings from the 1995-2010 reports and FY2011-FY2025. money_outWhat did the athletic fee fund pay for, line by line, in FY2020 to FY2022?MEASURED: the annual town reports print the fund's receipts, disbursements and year-end balance every year from FY2011 (FY2021: $176.22 spent, the balance rising to $296,286.42 at 30 June 2022), but not what it bought. The district itemised the fee-fund side only once, for FY14 to FY19, and the school journal held begins in FY2023. money_outWhat does Lunenburg pay, per child, for each place a resident child is schooled outside the district’s own schools?DESE publishes WHERE Lunenburg children are enrolled — 177 outside the district in FY2026 — and nothing about what any of them costs. A count of children is not a tuition, a charter assessment or a share of a regional assessment, and the general fund budget shows the appropriation rather than the fund each payment leaves. So the two halves of the question a resident actually asks — how many leave, and what that costs us — cannot be joined. — closes: DESE’s End of Year Financial Report for Lunenburg, which separates tuition and assessment spending by fund and by receiving district.
money_outWhat does a child arriving with an education plan cost Lunenburg's own schools, when the plan needs staff the budget did not carry?The ledger shows in-district special education as staff pay, by account, never by child, so an arrival's cost cannot be separated from the year's other changes. So when in-district special education runs over its budget, the surprise-costs page cannot say how much of the overrun was arrivals. — closes: the district's list of staff added mid-year for special education, each with the start date and the reason (an arrival, a plan change, a vacancy filled).
money_outWhat does one out-of-district placement cost Lunenburg in a year?DESE publishes what the district spent on tuition to private schools and collaboratives (functions 9300 and 9400), by fund, and the town publishes how many children were placed on 1 March. Nothing in this archive prices a single placement. /analysis/special-education-costs divides the first by the second and labels the result our estimate; /what-special-education-costs refuses to, and both are right about what the quotient is not: it mixes residential, day and collaborative places, it counts a child placed for part of a year as either a whole year or nothing depending on one day, and transportation is in a different line. A reserve for an unplanned placement needs the price of one, and the only figure available is that estimate. — closes: the accounts-payable detail behind general fund and fund 2640 accounts in functions 9300 and 9400 -- vendor, invoice period and amount, no student names -- from the Town Accountant, or the district's tuition rate sheets for the year.
money_outWhat does special education cost in Lunenburg all in, once the benefits and town-side costs of its staff are counted?The school MUNIS journal holds every posting to every school account in every fund, FY2023-FY2026, and /special-education/sped-all-funds sums the accounts the ledger labels special education across the general fund, the circuit breaker and the IDEA grants. That is the most complete view the archive holds and it is still a set of postings, not a cost: health insurance and other benefits are charged to school-wide or town accounts, not to a special education line, and special education work paid from accounts with no special education label (district-wide specialists, guidance, nurses) is not separable. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: the full cost of special education in any year. — closes: the district’s End of Year Financial Report, special education program, with benefits and town-side costs allocated by program.
money_outWhat does the FY2027 out-of-district tuition budget assume: which placements, for which months, and how much the circuit breaker will pay?The district's FY2027 workbook (budget-workbooks/fy27-proposals.xlsx) budgets $700,142 across private and collaborative tuition, the same figure in every scenario. The same two general-fund lines spent and committed $1,202,770.94 in FY2026 at period 13, and the circuit breaker fund (2640) paid $333,494.89 more. Placements ending, a larger circuit-breaker share, or FY2027 tuition paid in advance out of FY2026 money all fit, and the ledger cannot tell them apart. /analysis/fy26-school-surplus — closes: the FY2027 tuition worksheet (each placement anonymised: setting, rate, months, and the fund expected to pay it) and the service period of every FY2026 tuition invoice.
money_outWhat does the preschool cost the school budget, and what of it is the general fund?No school budget line, account, organization or program code is named for the preschool: the account codes place it inside the whole Primary School, and it is integrated, so children on education plans and tuition-paying children share its staff. Only the IDEA preschool grants (DESE codes 262, 264, 298) are identifiable, and our match of the annual report's preschool roster to its wage list gives pay, not cost, across every fund. Meanwhile the tuition is a Town receipt (general fund 431900), so nothing offsets the cost on the school side. — closes: a program cost report from the district listing preschool staff by FTE and the fund that pays each post, with the program's non-salary spending
money_outWhat each announced school position cut was worthOnly the FY2027 documents print a dollar figure beside a position. The FY2026 list the School Committee approved names 39 positions and prints no amount against any of them; the FY2025 impact slides print an FTE and a consequence and no money. So the register can say what was cut and, for one cycle in five, what it saved — and a figure beside a post is a budget-line saving, net of grants and fees (rule 11), rather than what the post costs. — closes: the personnel cost worksheet behind each year’s approved school budget, from the Business Office.
money_outWhat each of the town’s 500-odd accounting measures did before FY2026, line by line — the appropriation history of every department and the year-by-year activity of every fundThe registry (fund-owners.csv) lists every measure the FY26 reports print, but only the special-revenue funds have a read, tied history (FY2011–FY2023); the appropriation lines’ history sits in the annual reports where the extract cannot yet say which printed column is which, and FY2024–FY2025 fund activity was never printed — closes: the year-to-date budget reports and special-revenue reports for FY2023–FY2025 from the Town Accountant.
money_outWhat each town department was appropriated and spent in FY2024 and FY2025NARROWED 5 October 2026 for FY2024. the Finance Committee files received by records request on 4 October 2026 (sources/budget-workbooks/finance-committee/, see its PROVENANCE note) include a general fund budget-vs-actual history for every department, FY2010-FY2025, by MUNIS account (original, transfers, revised, actual). Its FY2025 column is part-year, so FY2025 stays open. Special revenue funds are not in it. The town published a General Fund Appropriations / Summary & Classification of Accounts schedule in every annual report through FY2023 — every department, appropriated against expended, with a printed GRAND TOTAL — and STOPPED. Its own contents pages show it: the FY2023 Accountant section lists the schedule and the General Fund Revenue and Expenditures charts; FY2024 lists a balance sheet, receivables, special revenue, capital, enterprise, trust and undesignated fund balance, and no appropriations at all; FY2025 is shorter again. FY2024 still prints the warrant’s FY 2025 Omnibus Budget, which is what was VOTED and not what was spent; FY2025 prints no department figures in any form, only Article 10’s total of $49,374,465.00 split across five funding sources. So for two consecutive years there is no published answer to what any single department was given or used — the question this archive answers for FY2011 through FY2023. — closes: the Town Accountant’s general fund appropriation and expenditure report for FY2024 and FY2025, the same schedule the annual report printed through FY2023, or the MUNIS year-end expense report by department for those years.
money_outWhat folding one athletics team would actually stop the town spendingA per-sport figure is not a saving. The district’s own workbook divides district-wide costs into thirds and pushes them into season totals — the notes column headed “Costs for all 3 Seasons” reads, at AX6, “MIAA 1/3 4550. -1516.67”, and at AY10 “MIDWACH - 1/3 7000 - 2333.33” — so league membership, trainer supplies, CPR certification and the online forms subscription sit inside per-sport totals. Whether any of those actually falls when one team folds is untested: a league assessment, a trainer’s hours and an insurance premium may each scale with the number of teams or not at all. This app answers it structurally rather than empirically — the FY27 athletics lines are split into a coaching-and-equipment pool that follows the teams and an overhead that does not, and the published per-sport figures are used only as weights to spread the pool — which bounds the saving without establishing it. — closes: the district’s athletics budget for a year in which a team was actually dropped, line by line against the year before, or a quotation from the MIAA and MIDWACH showing how each assessment varies with the number of teams entered.
